# Blueprint — Rick and Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

The working source is `index.html`, a single-file full-screen canvas game titled **Magnet Trick Run**. It is a physics-assisted side-scrolling stunt runner where a two-wheel board travels over procedural/custom terrain. The player uses mobile-friendly buttons for left, right, and **TRICK**. The board can drive on the ground, jump, spin in the air, land flips for score and coins, collect floating fuel pickups, buy upgrades, cycle themed maps, and enter an editor to place ramps or hazard/reward items.

The game uses a protected `requestAnimationFrame` loop with `updatePhysics(dt)` and `draw()`. It has states for `PLAYING`, `EDITOR`, `INGAME_SHOP`, `SETTINGS`, and `GAMEOVER`. Current hazards include gum, bomb, killbrick, tire spike, moving spike, metal spike, banana, ice path, and magma-map lava. Rewards include score, coins, flip bonuses, fuel, upgrades, jetpack, double jump, and magnet pickup.

## High-level code structure

- HTML/CSS UI overlays for HUD, controls, shop, settings, editor panel, media overlays, and game-over screen.
- Canvas gameplay rendering for terrain, board, collectibles, custom items, particles, popups, and map-specific effects.
- Audio elements and lightweight synth feedback.
- JSON-like `game-config` values for gravity, drive force, and spin force.
- State-management via `setState`.
- Map definitions with friction, drive multiplier, colors, and magma special behavior.
- Editor tool system that places ramps or items on the terrain.

## Game loop / state model

The loop runs continuously. During `PLAYING`, physics updates, score increments with ground movement, hazards/rewards resolve, and the camera follows the board. During menus/editor/game-over, gameplay physics pauses or changes interaction mode while drawing continues.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The player tries to ride forward, create air from terrain, rotate for flips, land safely, collect fuel/coins, survive hazards, and improve upgrades. Interaction is direct and mobile-first: hold left/right, tap/hold TRICK, tap HUD buttons, and use canvas taps/drag only for magnet/editor contexts.

## Inferred genre / gameplay shape

Medium-complexity arcade physics runner / stunt sandbox with light progression and item hazards.

## Current identity summary

The current presentation is bright arcade/Memphis/skater themed with maps named Sky Park, Frost Loop, Sunset Rush, and Nova Core. It already contains remote audio/GIF feedback and procedural canvas art, but it is not yet Rick and Morty-themed.

## Intended remixed trajectory

Transform the same protected stunt-runner into a **Rick and Morty-inspired portal-skate multiverse run**. Morty rides a jury-rigged hover-board through Rick’s unstable portal gauntlet, collecting portal charge, landing chaotic flips, and surviving dimension-specific hazards. The five-level arc should move from garage lab tutorial clarity to Citadel portal meltdown stakes.

## Preserve vs change guidance

### Preserve
- requestAnimationFrame main loop and update/draw separation
- PLAYING/EDITOR/INGAME_SHOP/SETTINGS/GAMEOVER state semantics
- left/right/TRICK input semantics and pointer-up reset behavior
- two-wheel board physics, distance constraint, terrain collision, gravity/friction/air drag
- jump, double jump, jetpack fuel behavior, and air spin torque
- flip detection and score/coin reward formulas
- ground movement score increment and high score storage
- hazard effects and failure semantics
- map button cycle behavior unless downstream explicitly creates safe variants
- shop costs/effects and settings volume/colorblind behavior
- mobile safe-area overlays and reachable buttons

### Change safely

- CSS color variables, panels, buttons, background gradients, particles
- canvas drawings for board, pickups, hazards, terrain textures, background dots
- map names and environmental interpretation
- HUD copy such as Score/Credits/Fuel/Run Over
- popup wording and reward/fail feedback language
- approved remote audio/GIF/image/font mapping from catalogs
- procedural background layers and decorative DOM/CSS overlays
- editor tool labels if effects stay identical

## Five-level trajectory

1. Garage Portal Warm-Up
2. Dimension C-137 Back-Alley Boost
3. Galactic Federation Checkpoint
4. Blips and Chitz Overdrive
5. Citadel Portal Meltdown

Each level should feel visually distinct while preserving controls, scoring, fail states, physics, and mobile actionability.

# Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
The current game is a compact single-file canvas arcade game in `index.html`.

- HTML defines a 400x600 `canvas`, score display, start overlay, game-over overlay, and mobile left/right controls.
- CSS provides a dark page, bordered glowing canvas, overlay panels, score styling, and touch-friendly circular control buttons.
- JavaScript owns all gameplay state and rendering:
  - `initGame()` resets the player, platforms, score, camera, and screen flags.
  - `createPlatform()` and `generatePlatforms()` create standard, moving, and breakable platforms.
  - `updatePlayer()`, `updatePlatforms()`, and `checkCollisions()` run the core arcade loop.
  - `drawBackground()`, `drawPlayer()`, and `drawPlatform()` draw primitive canvas visuals.
  - `gameLoop()` runs continuously through `requestAnimationFrame`.
  - keyboard and touch/mouse listeners map input to horizontal movement.

### Current gameplay heuristic
This is a Doodle Jump-style vertical platformer. The player controls a square jumper that automatically falls under gravity and bounces when landing on platforms. The player steers left/right to keep climbing while platforms scroll downward relative to the camera. The score increases as the player reaches higher vertical distance. Falling below the visible canvas triggers game over.

### Game loop / state model
The loop is continuous and always scheduled. Gameplay only updates while `gameStarted && !gameOver`.

1. Start overlay is visible.
2. Player presses Start.
3. `initGame()` creates a fresh run.
4. Each frame:
   - read horizontal input
   - apply gravity and velocity
   - wrap player horizontally
   - move camera upward when the player climbs
   - update/move/recycle platforms
   - check downward landing collisions
   - update score
   - draw background, platforms, player, score
5. If the player falls below the viewport, game over overlay appears with final score.
6. Restart repeats `initGame()`.

### Player goals
- Primary goal: climb as high as possible.
- Immediate goal: land on the next reachable platform.
- Survival goal: avoid falling below the screen.
- Score goal: maximize upward distance.

### Interaction pattern
- Keyboard: ArrowLeft/`A` and ArrowRight/`D` steer horizontally.
- Mobile/touch: left and right on-screen circular buttons.
- There is no jump button; bouncing is automatic on platform contact.

### Core systems
- Physics: simple velocity, gravity, bounce impulse.
- Camera: follows upward progress and converts climb into score.
- Platforms: generated at varied x/y positions with random standard, moving, or breakable behavior.
- Collision: player lands only while descending and crossing a platform from above.
- Game states: start, active play, game over.
- Rendering: canvas primitives and gradient/circle/star background.

### Current identity summary
The source identity is a generic neon/doodle arcade jumper with simple colors and abstract shapes. It does not yet express a specific authored world or character fiction.

# Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` is a self-contained HTML/CSS/JavaScript canvas game.
- CSS defines the full-screen shell, HUD, start screen, game-over screen, neon scanline/vignette styling, feedback GIF overlays, and mobile-safe viewport constraints.
- JavaScript defines:
  - `AudioSys`: catalog-backed remote audio playback plus oscillator music fallback.
  - Canvas setup and resize handling.
  - Protected state containers: `state`, `input`, `entities`, `player`.
  - Main systems: input listeners, reset/HUD updates, 3D projection, spawning, update loop, collision, particles, floor/gun/entity rendering, start/restart events.

### Game loop / state model
- Screen states: `start`, `playing`, `gameover`.
- The requestAnimationFrame loop always runs, but `update(dt)` only mutates gameplay while `state.screen === 'playing'`.
- `draw()` always renders the canvas world behind overlay states.
- `resetGame()` clears score, health, ammo, difficulty, streak, timers, player offsets, and entity arrays.
- `gameOver()` sets `screen` to `gameover`, pauses music, records final score, hides HUD, and shows the game-over overlay.

### Player goals
- Survive as long as possible in a forward 3D corridor.
- Destroy incoming enemies before they breach the center/player.
- Preserve shield/health and increase score.

### Interaction pattern
- Pointer/touch down starts continuous firing and enables drag steering.
- Pointer/touch movement changes `player.x` and `player.y`; this shifts projected world coordinates and aim lane.
- Releasing pointer stops firing and enables passive ammo regeneration after a delay.
- No explicit keyboard, pause, menu, or level-select controls are implemented.

### Core systems
- **Projection:** `project(x, y, z)` maps pseudo-3D positions into screen coordinates based on player offset and FOV.
- **Spawning:** random enemies appear at `SPAWN_DEPTH`; spawn chance increases with `state.difficulty`.
- **Enemy types:** cyan drones fly straight; orange hunters lerp toward player position.
- **Shooting:** bullets are created while input is down and ammo is available.
- **Ammo/reload:** 25 max ammo; depletion triggers timed reload; releasing input allows passive refill.
- **Collision:** bullet/enemy collisions compare z proximity and world-space x/y radius; enemy/player breach occurs near z < 50.
- **Scoring:** destroying enemies adds `100 * state.difficulty`; streak feedback triggers every 3 kills.
- **Failure:** health loses 20 per breach; zero health ends the run.
- **Rendering:** neon floor grid, enemies, bullets, particles, recoil gun, HUD, reticle, overlays.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
A mobile-friendly, first-person arcade wave-defense shooter with pseudo-3D corridor projection, hold-to-fire resource pressure, and escalating spawn/hunter pressure.

### Current identity summary
The current presentation is original neon/cyber corridor fiction: “Neon Drift Patrol,” prism rider, pulse lane, seekers, breach, shield, ammo, and score. It already uses procedural canvas shapes and a strong synthetic HUD.

## Intended remixed trajectory

### Remix-direction summary
The user prompt is `rick and morty`. The safe remix trajectory is a portal-chaos sci-fi version of the same corridor shooter: the player is not changing verbs or rules; they are piloting/aiming a portal stabilizer through interdimensional rifts while Rick-like mad-science gadgets, Morty-like anxious mission framing, portal rings, bug drones, Meeseeks-like helper silhouettes, and citadel/multiverse props replace the generic neon patrol identity.

### Preserve-vs-change guidance
Preserve:
- Input semantics: drag/touch to steer, hold/touch to fire, release to stop firing/passively reload.
- Main loop, update cadence, entity arrays, projection math, collision thresholds, ammo/reload timing, health damage, scoring formula, start/restart flow.
- Canvas rendering architecture and DOM HUD architecture.
- Mobile full-screen viewport and touch-action handling.
- Audio initialization requiring user gesture.

Change safely later:
- Copy: title, HUD labels, start/game-over text, button text.
- Canvas color palettes and procedural silhouettes.
- Enemy visual shape names and colors without changing type behavior.
- Background/gun/reticle styling.
- Feedback captions/GIF mapping only from approved catalogs.
- HUD styling and safe explanatory messaging.
- Conceptual level/world labels and non-invasive state messaging.

Do not change:
- Spawning model, enemy movement model, hunter tracking semantics, projectile mechanics, player bounds/sensitivity, scoring semantics, health loss, reload mechanics, screen-state behavior, or collision math during visual stages.

## Current game reality

The current game is **STREAM SHIELD**, a full-screen single-canvas arcade defense game. It uses a start screen, a playing state with HUD, and a game-over screen. Emoji enemies spawn at random horizontal positions above the screen, fall downward, and become faster, more frequent, and more durable over time. # Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

The current `index.html` implements **Mind Stone Sequence / Signal Sequence**, a mobile-first canvas memory ordering game. The player watches a short ordered sequence of numbered tiles during `MEMORIZE`, then the game shuffles those tiles into a lower pool during `INPUT`. The player taps tiles to place them into upper slots in the remembered order. A full set of slots triggers `CHECK`; a correct sequence awards score and advances the wave, while an incorrect sequence causes a shake/fail feedback and `GAMEOVER`.

### High-level code structure

- HTML shell with one full-screen `#game-container`.
- Canvas `#gameCanvas` is the gameplay surface.
- DOM HUD in `#ui-layer` displays score, wave, state messages, feedback GIFs, and game-over overlay.
- Hidden `#assets` block declares remote audio elements.
- `#game-config` JSON config exposes `baseTime`, `timePerTile`, `tileSpeed`, and `themeColor`.
- Inline JavaScript contains configuration parsing, state variables, audio/fallback systems, `Tile` and `Particle` classes, level initialization, input handling, resize handling, and the requestAnimationFrame loop.

### Game loop / state model

`LOADING -> MEMORIZE -> INPUT -> CHECK -> (success: next MEMORIZE) or GAMEOVER`.
The loop is protected and should not be rewritten.

### Player goals and interaction pattern

The goal is to reproduce a memorized order. The interaction is tap-only: tap a pool tile to send it to the next empty slot; tap a placed tile to return it to the pool before submitting. Submission is automatic when all slots are filled.

### Core systems

- Random unique sequence generation.
- Memorize timer bar.
- Tile lerp movement.
- Slot occupancy and ordering.
- Exact sequence comparison.
- Score and wave progression.
- Success/fail audio, GIF, vibration, particles, and game-over overlay.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The prompt is **“rick and morty”**. The safest remix is a Rick-and-Morty-inspired portal-code memory game, not a new action game. The existing tiles become portal coordinate cards, slots become portal stabilizer sockets, score becomes portal data, and waves become dimensions. The background should evolve across a five-world multiverse journey: garage calibration, warped street, Citadel court, Blips-and-Chitz arcade overload, and Central Finite Curve collapse.

# Recreation Prompt

Create a one-screen mobile-friendly arcade defense game called **Portal Base Defender: Rick and Morty Multiverse Swarm**.

A Rick-style garage portal core sits at the bottom center of a full-screen playfield. Small interdimensional parasites spill from unstable green portals along the top of the screen and travel toward the portal core. The player must tap or click each moving parasite before it reaches the core. Each defeated parasite awards **10 points**. If a parasite reaches the portal core, **portal stability** drops by **10**. When portal stability reaches zero, stop the action and show a full-screen game-over overlay with collapse-themed copy, the final score, and a restart button. Restart must reset score, stability, active enemies, and spawning.

Preserve the source structure: direct tap/click target removal, a bottom-center base, enemy movement toward that base, score survival, health/stability depletion on contact, game over at zero stability, and restart. Do not add movement controls, projectile aiming, towers, inventory, upgrades, dialogue choices, or new win/loss conditions.

Use a procedural cartoon sci-fi presentation inspired by Rick and Morty without depending on copyrighted image assets. Draw the identity through CSS/SVG/DOM shapes: green portal rings, garage lab silhouettes, Morty panic signage, Cronenberg slime and mutation veins, Cromulon cosmic heads in the far background, Citadel server towers, and Galactic Federation warning stripes. Enemies should remain large, high-contrast, and easy to tap on mobile.

Frame progression as five conceptual worlds:
1. **Garage Portal Breach** — readable baseline portal-defense loop.
2. **Cronenberg Alley Spillover** — mutated suburb palette and mild pressure.
3. **Cromulon Broadcast Zone** — cosmic stage spectacle and full intended loop.
4. **Citadel Server Stack** — tech-fortress visuals and higher incoming pressure.
5. **Galactic Federation Collapse** — final red-alert multiverse breakdown.

Difficulty should escalate only through existing safe dimensions such as spawn cadence, enemy speed range, simultaneous target count, and visual stakes. Keep mechanics stable, keep targets readable, and make the animated background secondary to gameplay.

# Blueprint — Rick and Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

The implemented game is **Base Defender: Ant Smash**, a simple one-screen arcade defense game built in a single `index.html`. It uses DOM elements, CSS, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame`.

### High-level code structure
- HTML contains a full-viewport `#game-container`, a health bar, a score display, a bottom-centered `.base`, a hidden game-over overlay, and a restart button.
- CSS defines the garden-like background, ant shapes, base shape, HUD, and game-over overlay.
- Inline JavaScript stores `score`, `health`, `gameActive`, and `antInterval`.
- `createAnt()` spawns an enemy at a random top x-position, draws legs, computes a direction toward the base, animates it, and attaches the click handler.
- `moveAnt()` advances each enemy and checks DOM rectangle overlap with the base.
- `updateHealth()`, `updateScore()`, `endGame()`, and `restartGame()` manage feedback and state reset.

### Game loop / state model
1. Active play begins immediately.
2. Every second, an ant is spawned.
3. Each ant moves from the top toward the bottom-center base.
4. The player clicks/taps ants to remove them for +10 score.
5. If an ant reaches the base, it deals 10 health damage and is removed.
6. At 0 health, active play stops and the game-over overlay appears.
7. Restart resets score, health, enemies, and spawning.

### Player goals
- Primary: keep the base alive.
- Secondary: achieve the highest possible score.

### Interaction pattern
The only gameplay input is direct pointer interaction with moving targets. The only menu/overlay input is the restart button.

### Core systems
- Enemy spawning and randomization.
- Direct tap/click enemy removal.
- Target movement toward a fixed base.
- Base collision and health damage.
- Score and final score feedback.
- Restart/reset.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
Simple one-screen arcade tap-defense / survival-score game.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The user prompt is `rick and morty`. The safest and clearest transformation is:

**Portal Base Defender: Rick and Morty Multiverse Swarm** — Rick's garage portal core sits at the bottom of the playfield while interdimensional parasites spill from unstable portals above. The player taps each parasite before it reaches the portal core. Score becomes dimension seals or escaped dimensions; health becomes portal stability.

This remix should be recognizable through portal-green energy, Rick garage lab silhouettes, Morty panic signage, Cronenberg mutation motifs, Cromulon cosmic show imagery, Citadel tech, and Galactic Federation warning graphics.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- Direct click/tap on moving targets.
- +10 score per cleared target.
- Base health damage on contact.
- Game over at zero health.
- Restart behavior.
- Enemy movement toward the bottom-center base.
- DOM/requestAnimationFrame/collision architecture.
- Mobile-friendly target size and tap semantics.

### Change safely
- Title, HUD wording, and overlay copy.
- Ant visuals into portal parasites / alien bugs.
- Base visuals into Rick's garage portal core.
- Static stock-like background into procedural animated Rick and Morty-inspired worlds.
- Health bar styling into portal stability.
- Score styling into dimension seals/approval/patches.
- Cosmetic particles and state-reactive background cues.

## Remix-direction summary
Downstream stages should strengthen theme primarily through procedural visual identity, authored world framing, HUD copy, and five conceptual world beats. Mechanics should remain untouched unless a later stage is explicitly deriving level variants through safe existing knobs.

## Required v4 planning keys
The complete structured planning contract is in `remix_plan_v4.json` and includes:
- `mechanic_decomposition`
- `complexity_profile`
- `protected_mechanics`
- `safe_theming_surfaces`
- `remix_premise`
- `one_point_five_level_core`
- `five_level_difficulty_progression`
- `five_level_visual_evolution`
- `procedural_art_system`
- `downstream_stage_contract`

# Blueprint — Remix v4 Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` contains all runtime code, styles, markup, asset declarations, configuration, and canvas rendering.
- The game uses a single `<canvas id="gameCanvas">` with DOM HUD overlays.
- CSS defines the HUD, modal game-over shell, feedback banners/GIF overlay, and responsive mobile behavior.
- Inline JavaScript owns state, input, spawning, scoring, audio unlock/playback, particles, procedural terrain, and rendering.

### Game loop / state model
- States present in code: `BOOT`, `PLAYING`, `GAMEOVER`.
- `DOMContentLoaded` initializes the canvas, parses `game-config`, calls `initGame()`, immediately sets state to `PLAYING`, starts background audio opportunistically, and starts `requestAnimationFrame(loop)`.
- `loop(timestamp)` caps delta time, runs `update(dt)` only in `PLAYING`, then always runs `draw()`.
- `GAMEOVER` UI exists and restart works, but the current update loop does not appear to trigger `setState('GAMEOVER')`; wrong collections reduce score rather than ending play.

### Player goals
- Read the active target region in the HUD.
- Move the aircraft horizontally to collect falling location labels that belong to that target region.
- Avoid or ignore falling labels from other regions because collecting them subtracts score.
- Build the highest route score while target region, spawn cadence, and day/night background continue cycling.

### Interaction pattern
- Pointer/touch down and pointer/touch move set `hero.targetX`.
- The hero smoothly eases horizontally toward the target x-position.
- No jump, fire, drag/drop, lane switch button, menu routing, or multi-action controls are present.
- Restart button is available only on the existing game-over overlay.

### Core systems
- **Input:** pointer position maps to horizontal target.
- **Movement:** fixed vertical hero position with smoothed lateral movement.
- **Spawning:** one falling item every variable interval; interval decreases with score down to a floor.
- **Classification:** active region maps to a list of valid country/location names.
- **Collision:** radial distance between item center and hero center.
- **Scoring:** +10 for valid collection, -5 for invalid collection with floor at 0.
- **Progression:** score accelerates spawn interval; target region changes every 20 seconds; day/night cycles continuously.
- **Rendering:** scrolling map image, night brightness filter, procedural clouds/mountains, procedural plane, text-bubble items, particles, vignette.
- **Feedback:** HUD, feedback banner/GIF, sound effects, haptics.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
The source is a simple one-screen arcade collection/avoidance runner. It behaves like a vertical scrolling route-matching game: a horizontally controlled hero catches correct falling targets and avoids incorrect ones.

### Current identity summary
Current title and framing are travel/flight themed: `Aero Geo: World Tour`. The player pilots a stylized plane and logs countries matching a displayed continent/region.

### Intended remixed trajectory
The remix prompt is `rick and morty`. The safest intended transformation is a Rick-and-Morty-inspired multiverse portal courier arcade game:
- The plane becomes a portal cruiser / flying saucer silhouette.
- Continents become portal sectors or dimensions.
- Country labels become dimension IDs, aliens, artifacts, or timeline coordinates.
- Correct collection means stabilizing the currently tracked portal frequency.
- Wrong collection means grabbing an off-frequency universe sample.
- The scrolling world becomes an animated portal tunnel / Citadel / dimension chain.
- HUD becomes a sci-fi portal gun dashboard.
- Difficulty and progression remain based on the existing collection/avoidance loop.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- Pointer/touch input semantics.
- Horizontal smoothing movement.
- Falling item spawn/update/collision loop.
- Score semantics: correct +10, wrong -5, floor at 0.
- Region/target matching concept.
- Region timer concept.
- Day/night/progress-cycle style timing unless only cosmetically reframed.
- Existing one-screen mobile-first canvas structure.
- Audio unlock pattern and nonblocking media failure behavior.

### Change safely later
- Text/copy labels from travel language to portal/multiverse language.
- `CONTINENTS` data labels to Rick-and-Morty-adjacent but non-media-dependent dimension sectors.
- Procedural visual rendering of hero, item bubbles, terrain, background, particles, HUD styling.
- Asset mappings to approved catalog remote media only, if media is used.
- UI wording and feedback banner strings.
- Cosmetic progression indicators and level titles.
- Optional safe config tuning only if downstream runtime verification proves playability.

### Do not change in downstream stages
- Do not rewrite the main loop.
- Do not replace the collision model.
- Do not add weapons, enemies, health, inventory, or dialogue trees.
- Do not make the player stop to answer quizzes.
- Do not make mobile input multi-touch or button-heavy.
- Do not introduce a new loss condition unless explicitly required and safely verified.

  - config parsing from `#game-config`,

### Game loop / state model
1. Game initializes after the canvas resize observer receives dimensions.

4. Player taps `Start Chemistry Test ♥`.

# RecreationPrompt.md

Create a mobile-friendly top-down arcade survival collection game called **Rick and Morty: Portal Panic Supply Run**.

The player controls a small Morty-like runner on a full-screen canvas by moving the mouse or dragging/touching toward a target. Morty moves around a circular unstable pocket-dimension arena while the camera smoothly follows. The objective is to survive as long as possible and collect the highest number of portal parts.

Keep the original arcade loop simple and readable:
- Touch or mouse movement steers Morty toward the target.
- Collect regular portal coils for 10 points.
- Collect isotope crystal chunks for 20 points.
- Collect mega-seed snacks to restore hunger but not score.
- Avoid alien crab-like patrol bugs or Council drones; contact damages stamina and knocks the player back.
- Hunger slowly drains over time. When hunger is empty, stamina drains until game over.
- Show a start instructions card, an in-game HUD, a game-over score card, and restart.

The presentation should feel like an absurd Rick-and-Morty-style portal emergency without changing the mechanics. Use procedural cartoon sci-fi art: green portal rings, lab sparks, scanner grids, Citadel silhouettes, Morty's yellow shirt, anxious character expressions, alien patrol hazards, isotope crystals, mega seeds, and bold neon outlines. The HUD should feel like Rick's scanner with stamina, hunger, and portal-parts score.

Plan the world as five visually distinct dimensions that share the same mechanics:
1. Garage Rift Beach — stable portal lab/island hybrid.
2. Cronenberg Tide — organic mutation creeps around the arena.
3. Citadel Scrap Orbit — floating towers and portal debris.
4. Cromulon Broadcast Storm — giant broadcast silhouettes and wave rings.
5. Council of Ricks Meltdown — final green portal vortex with emergency lighting.

Preserve mobile actionability, collision readability, high-score survival, and the original collect/avoid/hunger/stamina semantics. Do not add shooting, inventory, dialogue choices, or new combat systems.

# Blueprint.md

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
The workspace currently contains a single playable `index.html` with embedded CSS and JavaScript. The implementation uses:
- DOM/CSS overlays for the start screen, game-over screen, HUD, bars, buttons, and reaction GIFs.
- A full-window canvas for the active playfield.
- An `AudioController` class for remote BGM/SFX playback after user gesture unlock.
- Procedural Canvas drawing functions for the island, ocean bands, player, resources, enemies, and particles.
- A protected `requestAnimationFrame` game loop.

### Game loop / state model
The game has three primary states:
1. Start/instructions screen.
2. Active run with HUD visible.
3. Game-over/results screen with restart.

Clicking **Start Run** unlocks audio, hides the start screen, initializes score/player/resources/enemies, and starts the loop. Game over occurs when HP/stamina reaches zero. Restart resets the run.

### Player goals
The player steers around a circular island collecting supplies for score while managing hunger and avoiding crab patrol enemies. The run is open-ended and high-score based.

### Interaction pattern
Mouse movement or touch movement sets a world-space target. While input is active, the avatar moves toward that target. Resources are collected by contact. Enemies damage the player on contact. Berries restore hunger.

### Core systems
- Pointer/touch target movement.
- Camera follow over a larger circular world.
- Random resource and enemy spawning inside island radius.
- Circle-overlap collision detection.
- Score, hunger, and stamina HUD.
- Contact damage, hunger drain, resource pickup, particle feedback, reaction GIFs, and audio cues.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
A mobile-friendly top-down survival collection arcade loop: collect rewards, route around hazards, watch survival meters, and chase a high score.

## Intended remixed trajectory

### Remix direction summary
The prompt `rick and morty` should transform the beach supply run into **Rick and Morty: Portal Panic Supply Run**. Morty scavenges portal stabilizer parts across unstable pocket dimensions while Rick appears through HUD/scanner styling. Crabs become alien patrol bugs or council drones. Trees, rocks, and berries become portal coils, isotope crystals, and mega-seed snacks.

### Preserve-vs-change guidance
Preserve:
- Input semantics.
- Movement, camera, and circular bounds.
- Spawn, pickup, collision, damage, and scoring semantics.
- Hunger and stamina meanings.
- Start, game-over, and restart flow.
- Mobile-safe HUD/button structure.

Change safely:
- Copy, title, instructions, labels, and icons.
- Procedural drawing of player, enemies, resources, and background.
- CSS colors, HUD theming, and portal scanner presentation.
- Reaction media/audio mapping only via approved catalog URLs in later stages.
- Conceptual level/world framing.

### Downstream priority
Make the game unmistakably Rick-and-Morty-inspired through procedural sci-fi portal art and authored world layers, not through risky new mechanics. The five-level plan should be implemented as presentation-first world progression with only conservative difficulty tuning when safe.

# Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

`index.html` implements **Magnet Trick Run**, a single-file HTML/CSS/Canvas physics stunt runner. The player controls a two-wheel board over procedural and editor-authored terrain using mobile-first buttons: **left**, **right**, and **TRICK**. The core loop is to keep moving, jump from terrain, rotate in the air, land clean flips, collect fuel, avoid hazards, and spend coins on upgrades.

### High-level code structure

- Inline CSS establishes a full-screen canvas, safe-area-aware HUD, bottom mobile controls, editor panel, shop modal, settings modal, game-over modal, and feedback GIF overlays.
- Inline config JSON exposes three physics knobs: `gravity`, `driveForce`, and `spinForce`.
- Inline JavaScript manages:
  - state machine: `PLAYING`, `EDITOR`, `INGAME_SHOP`, `SETTINGS`, `GAMEOVER`
  - audio unlock and mapped remote SFX/BGM
  - map definitions: Sky Park, Frost Loop, Sunset Rush, Nova Core
  - board physics with two constrained wheels
  - custom terrain ramps and custom item placement
  - collectibles, particles, popups, upgrades, hazards, magma eruption, magnet behavior
  - Canvas drawing for terrain, items, board, particles, HUD popups

## Game loop / state model

`gameLoop()` calls `updatePhysics(dt)` only during `PLAYING`, increments score while the board moves on ground, then calls `draw()` every frame. UI state is controlled by `setState()`, which shows or hides HUD, controls, editor, shop, settings, magma HUD, and game-over panels.

## Player goals

1. Keep the board alive and on/near terrain.
2. Build forward score by riding.
3. Earn high-value score/coins by landing flips cleanly.
4. Collect fuel pickups and use upgrades to extend stunt capability.
5. Avoid or recover from hazards.
6. Optionally use the editor to place terrain and item challenges.

## Interaction pattern

- Hold **left/right** to drive on ground or spin in air.
- Press **TRICK** to jump; with upgrades it can double-jump or sustain jetpack thrust; while stuck in gum it functions as a struggle input.
- Press/tap canvas with an equipped magnet to attract metal spikes.
- Use **ZONE** to cycle maps.
- Use editor/shop/settings buttons for secondary systems.

## Core systems

- Protected board physics and terrain contact
- Terrain ramp displacement via `getTerrainY`
- Score/coin rewards from distance and flips
- Fuel pickup/jetpack resource
- Shop upgrades
- Zone-specific physics/timing modifiers
- Editor-authored ramps and hazards
- Canvas procedural rendering

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape

A **medium-complexity side-scrolling physics stunt runner** with timing-heavy stunt scoring, mobile arcade controls, sandbox challenge placement, and light upgrade/resource progression.

## Current identity summary

The current presentation is bright Memphis/comic arcade stunt riding with generic zones, skateboard/hoverboard visuals, procedural terrain, colorful hazards, remote audio, and feedback GIF overlays.

## Remix-direction summary: Rick and Morty

The active remix prompt is `rick and morty`. The safe target is a portal-science multiverse stunt runner: a Rick-and-Morty-inspired garage experiment sends the rider through unstable dimensions while preserving the exact board physics, controls, scoring, hazards, maps, editor, and shop semantics.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve

- Core game loop
- Two-wheel board physics
- Terrain/collision model
- Mobile controls and input semantics
- Score/coin/high-score semantics
- Flip landing rules
- Upgrade costs/effects
- Hazard outcomes
- Existing state machine
- Runtime stability of `index.html`

### Change safely downstream

- Title/copy/HUD wording
- Colors, procedural backgrounds, props, particles
- Map names and visual identities
- Hazard/reward visual interpretation
- Shop/editor label copy
- Supplemental catalog-approved media mapping

### Do not overinterpret

Do not add shooter mechanics, dialogue-choice systems, RPG progression, combat, inventory, or story cutscenes. The remix should remain a physics stunt runner, not become a new genre.

# Blueprint: Portal Rival Rush Remix Inference

## Current game reality

The current codebase is a single-file browser game in `index.html`. It uses Three.js for a full-screen 3D scene, inline CSS for a neon mobile HUD, and inline JavaScript for input, roster generation, fighter entities, AI, audio, and screen-state transitions.

The implemented game is a mobile-first one-on-one arena fighter. The player starts at a title card, opens character select, chooses a fighter from a generated roster, and enters a duel against a randomly selected opponent. The player controls a fighter with a virtual joystick plus three touch buttons: JUMP, ATK, and KICK. The duel is resolved by HP and a 99-second timer. The player wins when `p1.hp > p2.hp` at the end of the round and loses otherwise.

## High-level code structure

- CSS utility classes and mobile layout rules.
- UI DOM: start screen, character select, HUD, result screen, joystick, action buttons, reaction GIF overlays.
- `ASSETS`: remote audio and GIF URLs.
- `FIGHTERS`: roster data with type, color, power, speed, hair, weapon, outfit.
- `audio`: BGM/stinger/SFX wrapper with unlock and loop control.
- `VirtualJoystick`: touch/mouse joystick updating `input.x` and `input.y`.
- Three.js scene setup: camera, renderer, lights, city, floor, grid.
- Procedural generators: hair and weapon geometry.
- `Fighter3D`: visual construction, physics, movement, jump, attack, hit reaction, damage, disposal.
- Game logic: character select, `startGame`, `updateHUD`, `endGame`, AI update, animation loop, UI bindings.

## Game loop / state model

1. Start screen waits for START RUN.
2. Character select generates hero/rival buttons and waits for fighter selection.
3. `startGame` creates player and rival fighters, shows HUD and controls, starts timer and BGM.
4. `animate` polls input, moves/attacks/jumps, updates AI, updates fighters, tracks camera, and renders.
5. Damage updates HP. HP reaching 0 or timer reaching 0 calls `endGame`.
6. Result screen shows win/loss copy and restart returns to character select.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The player tries to stay in range long enough to hit the rival while avoiding being hit. The interaction is spacing, timing, and cooldown management, not combo complexity. Character stats create different movement and damage profiles. The AI chases when far and randomly attacks when near.

## Core systems

- Protected input: virtual joystick and tap buttons.
- Protected physics: x-axis movement, y-axis jump/gravity, friction, arena bounds.
- Protected combat: punch/kick cooldown, delayed hit check, range/y-distance, power-scaled damage.
- Protected win/loss: HP and timer comparison.
- Themable systems: roster names/colors/shapes, city background, floor grid, HUD copy, audio/GIF choices, result messages.

## Current identity summary

The current identity is `Neon Rival Rush`, a cyber street-circuit brawler with neon city skyline, generic fighters, HP bars, a timer, and arcade audio/feedback.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The remix prompt is `rick and morty`. The intended result should become a Rick-and-Morty-inspired dimension-hopping 1v1 portal brawler named `Portal Rival Rush`. The existing duel becomes a portal-stability showdown between garage scientists, family allies, variants, mutants, federation agents, and citadel rivals. The arena evolves across five conceptual dimensions while the core mechanics remain intact.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

Preserve:
- Game loop and render architecture.
- Joystick/buttons and mobile safe areas.
- Fighter physics, attack range, cooldowns, HP damage, AI basics, timer, result semantics.
- Full-screen single-arena camera assumptions.

Change safely:
- Title/copy and HUD labels.
- Roster names and visual traits.
- Procedural character materials and silhouettes.
- Background props from neon city to portal garage, Cronenberg alley, Citadel, Federation starport, and collapsing curve.
- Audio/GIF URLs only from approved catalogs.
- Visual feedback and motion graphics that do not block play.

# Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality
The codebase is a single-file HTML5 canvas game (`index.html`) with inline CSS and JavaScript. It implements a portrait/mobile-first resource-management farming loop called **AgriGrid Command**. A DOM UI layer supplies start/end screens, top HUD, bottom seed selector, sound and store controls, and a store modal. The canvas renders six vertical plot lanes, plot state colors/icons, progress bars, particles, and floating reward/error text.

## High-level code structure
- CSS reset, utility classes, HUD/card/button styling, reaction GIF placements, and mobile adjustments.
- DOM UI: HUD money, store/sound buttons, tractor/rig display, seed selector, store modal, start screen, end modal, callout, GIF badges, canvas.
- Game configuration: `CROPS`, `CONFIG`, `MEDIA`.
- Audio system: SFX and loops gated by user gesture on start.
- Feedback system: GIF flashes and HUD callouts.
- Core game state: money, seed inventory, selected seed, tractor count, plots, particles, floaters, timing flags.
- `Plot` class: protected state machine for locked/empty/sowing/growing/ready/harvesting.
- Input/store/HUD/win/loss/reset/loop/resize initialization functions.

## Game loop / state model
The player starts from a title screen, enters play, buys packets in the store, selects one packet type, taps an empty plot to plant, waits through sowing and growing timers, taps a ready plot to harvest, earns money, unlocks more lanes, buys speed upgrades, and repeats. Victory occurs at $5,000. Loss occurs only when the player has less money than the cheapest seed, no seeds, and no active crop.

## Player goals
- Immediate: keep crop lanes cycling and avoid wasting money.
- Mid-term: unlock additional lanes and upgrade processing speed.
- Final: reach the $5,000 quota.

## Interaction pattern
Tap/click canvas lanes for locked-lane purchase, empty-lane planting, and ready-lane harvesting. Tap DOM controls for start, store, purchases, seed selection, sound toggle, close modal, and restart.

## Core systems
- Timed plot progression
- Seed inventory
- Money economy
- Crop ROI tiers
- Lane unlock ladder
- Tractor/rig speed upgrade ladder
- Win/loss checks
- Audio/visual feedback

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape
A mobile farm tycoon / resource-management clicker with light idle timing and lane servicing.

## Current identity summary
The current presentation is an agro-tech farm command fantasy using crop emoji, tractor/drone labels, sky panels, rural gradients, and store/field language.

## Intended remixed trajectory
Transform the presentation into **Portal Harvest Command**, a Rick-and-Morty-inspired multiverse portal harvest tycoon. Crop lanes become unstable portal lanes, seeds become dimension packets, money becomes portal credits, tractor upgrades become portal rig boosts, and the store becomes a garage lab terminal. The player helps a reckless scientist and anxious sidekick harvest alien specimens across five escalating dimensions while preserving the tap/economy loop.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance
### Preserve
- Canvas loop and plot state machine
- Tap lane input and DOM button semantics
- Money/seed/upgrade/unlock/win/loss rules
- Mobile-safe six-lane vertical layout
- Store modal purchase flow
- Audio initialization behavior

### Change safely
- Copy, labels, icons, color palette, callouts, title/end messages
- Procedural CSS/canvas background identity
- Crop names/icons as long as tiers remain clear
- Store theme and HUD language
- Particle colors and non-interactive ambient motion

### Avoid
- Adding combat, enemies, movement, physics, projectile aiming, or new gestures
- Replacing the resource-management loop with an unrelated franchise scene
- Broad JS refactors or collision/input changes
- Media use outside approved catalogs

# Blueprint — Rick and Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current Game Reality

### High-Level Code Structure
The game is implemented as a single-page HTML canvas arcade game in `index.html`.

Key sections:
- CSS variables and UI styling define a neon sci-fi HUD, modal panels, and responsive mobile layout.
- Hidden audio/media declarations provide BGM and SFX elements with remote URLs and fallback synthesis.
- `window.gameConfigDefs` / `window.gameConfig` expose safe numeric knobs: `heroSpeed`, `fireRate`, `enemySpawnRate`, and `themeColor`.
- `AudioManager` handles BGM, SFX playback, audio unlocking, and synthesized fallback tones.
- `Game` owns canvas setup, state, entities, input, update loop, drawing, spawning, scoring, collisions, and UI transitions.

### Game Loop / State Model
The implemented state model is:
1. `MENU` — centered start panel is visible; canvas renders background/hero.
2. `PLAYING` — start panel hidden, HUD visible, gameplay systems update.
3. `GAMEOVER` — game-over panel visible with final score and restart button.

The main loop is a `requestAnimationFrame` loop that calls `update(dt)` and `draw()` every frame.

### Player Goals
The player tries to:
- Survive enemy swarms.
- Keep hull HP above zero.
- Destroy enemies automatically by positioning near them.
- Collect star shards dropped by destroyed enemies.
- Maximize final score.

### Interaction Pattern
The game is one-thumb/mobile-friendly:
- Pointer/touch down activates movement.
- Dragging or holding sets a target position.
- The hero moves toward that pointer.
- Shooting is automatic; the player does not manually aim or fire.
- Restart uses the same start/reset routine.

### Core Systems
- **Movement:** hero follows pointer at fixed speed and is clamped to viewport.
- **Auto-combat:** hero finds nearest enemy within range and fires on a cooldown.
- **Spawning:** enemies spawn from random screen edges at fixed frame intervals.
- **Enemy chase:** enemies move toward the hero and separate slightly from each other.
- **Collision:** circular distance checks handle bullet hits, enemy contact, and shard pickup.
- **Rewards:** defeated enemies drop collectible shards that drift and magnetize to the hero.
- **Scoring:** each collected shard gives +1.
- **Damage:** enemy overlap drains hull HP.
- **Feedback:** particles, floating numbers, screen shake, hit/fail badges, HUD updates, BGM/SFX.
- **Rendering:** Canvas 2D procedural art with a space grid, stars, hero saucer, enemies, bullets, shards, particles, and text.

### Inferred Genre / Gameplay Shape
The source game is a medium-complexity one-screen arcade survival shooter with:
- drag movement,
- automatic shooting,
- chasing hazards,
- collection scoring,
- HP attrition,
- endless score pursuit.

It is not currently a multi-level game. There is no explicit win condition.

### Current Identity Summary
The existing identity is `Star Survivor: Orbital Sweep`: a neon space arena where a small nova skimmer fights drones, recovers star shards, and protects hull integrity.

## Intended Remixed Trajectory

### Remix Prompt Interpretation
The prompt `rick and morty` should transform the presentation into a chaotic portal-sci-fi comedy survival game while preserving the implemented loop. The safest and strongest mapping is:

> Pilot Rick's portal saucer with Morty in the cockpit through unstable dimensions, auto-zapping hostile anomalies and collecting portal shards before the hull gives out.

### Target Title
**Rick and Morty: Portal Shard Sweep**

### Target Identity
A procedural Rick-and-Morty-inspired portal survival shooter:
- Player craft: Rick's improvised portal saucer/skimmer.
- Co-pilot flavor: Morty panic shown through UI copy, cockpit details, and warning text.
- Hazards: Cronenberg blobs, Federation drones, Meeseeks echoes, Citadel guard cores.
- Rewards: portal shards, microverse batteries, finite-curve fragments.
- Backgrounds: garage portal, Cronenberg alley, Federation grid, Meeseeks chamber, Citadel collapse.

### Preserve-vs-Change Guidance

#### Preserve
These mechanics are protected and should not be changed by downstream presentation stages:
- Pointer drag movement.
- Automatic nearest-target shooting.
- Enemy edge spawning.
- Runner/tank enemy type roles.
- Enemy chase movement.
- Circle collision model.
- HP loss on enemy contact.
- Game over at HP <= 0.
- Enemy death dropping one collectible.
- Magnetized collection behavior.
- +1 score per collected shard.
- MENU / PLAYING / GAMEOVER state flow.
- Responsive full-screen canvas.
- One-thumb mobile operation.

#### Safe to Change
These surfaces can be transformed safely:
- Game title, subtitle, instructions, buttons, score labels, and result copy.
- HUD visual style and labels.
- CSS colors, panel treatments, fonts, glows, and background overlays.
- Canvas art for hero, enemies, bullets, collectibles, particles, and world motifs.
- Audio labels or catalog-approved audio selections in later stages.
- Background motif system and animated procedural scenery.
- Conceptual level framing and difficulty documentation.

#### Avoid
Downstream stages should not:
- Add manual shooting.
- Add new buttons required during play.
- Add new enemy attack patterns.
- Rewrite physics, collisions, or the main loop.
- Introduce scrolling maps or complex menus.
- Make level progression depend on risky routing logic.
- Use external images as the main identity if procedural art can carry the theme.

## Five-Level Planning Summary
Even though the current game is endless, the remix can support five conceptual worlds:

1. **Garage Portal Calibration** — base loop, cleanest version, stable green portal and lab props.
2. **Cronenberg Back Alley** — clearer hazard pressure, biological mutants and purple-green residue.
3. **Federation Drone Grid** — full intended stack, scanner grid and drone patrol identity.
4. **Meeseeks Box Overload** — same loop under greater visual/spacing pressure, blue pop-ring chaos.
5. **Citadel Central Finite Curve** — finale pressure, Citadel skyline and collapsing portal vortex.

Difficulty should come from existing knobs and presentation clarity, not new mechanics.

## 1.5-Level Core
The smallest proof of scalable remix:
- **Level 1:** reskin the current loop into Rick's garage portal shard sweep.
- **Level 1.5:** retain the same mechanics but make enemy type distinction and portal instability more pronounced, proving the loop can become more intense without new controls or rules.

## Downstream Priority
1. Replace generic space identity with portal-garage/Cronenberg/Federation/Meeseeks/Citadel procedural motifs.
2. Preserve core mechanics exactly.
3. Improve readability and mobile-safe HUD.
4. Use five-level visual evolution if later stages introduce variants.
5. Verify runtime only on the assigned validation URL/port when browser validation is required.

# Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality
`index.html` is a complete single-file mobile-first canvas/DOM game. CSS defines the full-screen glass/neon UI, start screen, game-over screen, HUD, feedback overlays, responsive button sizing, and canvas sizing. Inline JavaScript defines assets, an `AudioController`, scenario data, score and Signal/Social Battery state, procedural background particles, canvas chat rendering, input handlers, start/restart flow, and the animation loop.

## Implemented genre / archetype
The implemented game is a simple one-screen interactive chat-choice arcade / score-survival game. The player receives random chat scenarios and taps one of two answer buttons. Safe answers add score and preserve the Signal/Social Battery; risky answers may reduce the battery. There is no movement, physics, aiming, inventory, branching map, or explicit level system.

## Game loop / state model
1. Start screen is shown.
2. Player taps `OPEN CHANNEL`.
3. Audio unlocks, HUD appears, `gameActive` becomes true, score and battery reset.
4. A random scenario from `SCENARIOS` is selected.
5. An incoming chat bubble appears.
6. Two large answer buttons are drawn on the canvas.
7. Player taps/clicks one answer.
8. The selected reply is appended as an Operator bubble.
9. `score += option.s`; `socialBattery += option.d`; battery is capped at 100.
10. Success/failure audio and feedback captions/GIFs play.
11. After a 1000 ms delay, another random scenario appears if battery is above zero.
12. If battery reaches zero or below, game over appears with the final score.
13. Restart resets and repeats the same loop.

## Player goals and controls
The goal is to keep the channel stable as long as possible and earn the highest score. The core verb is tapping/clicking one of two responses. Start and restart are DOM buttons with click and touchend handlers. Gameplay response buttons are canvas hitboxes with mouse and touchstart handling. Mobile actionability is already central to the implementation.

## Screen states likely present
- Start screen.
- Active gameplay with HUD, canvas chat feed, answer buttons, and feedback overlays.
- Game-over screen.
- Restarted gameplay state.

## Current identity summary
The source identity is `Crisis Chat Control`: a futuristic social-message crisis game with neon blue/purple gradients, signal language, a phone-like chat frame, score, and Signal/Social Battery.

## Intended remixed trajectory: Rick and Morty
Transform presentation into `Portal Panic: Multiverse Chat Control`, a Rick-and-Morty-style interdimensional portal-comms crisis game. The player acts as the emergency operator for Rick's unstable portal inbox, choosing the least catastrophic reply to messages from Rick, Morty, Summer, Beth, Jerry, the Council of Ricks, Mr. Meeseeks, Birdperson, aliens, parasites, scammers, and alternate-dimension contacts.

The core play remains exactly the same: random incoming message, two replies, tap one, score/stability update, feedback, and collapse at zero stability.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- One-screen canvas/DOM architecture.
- Start → play → game over → restart state flow.
- Two-choice tap/click input semantics.
- Random scenario queue.
- Score addition semantics.
- Battery/stability damage semantics and game-over threshold.
- 1000 ms next-scenario pacing unless a later stage documents a tiny safe tuning change.
- Responsive button layout and mobile touch handlers.
- Canvas message-bubble rendering structure.
- HUD with stability meter and score.

### Change safely
- Title, subtitle, status chips, button labels, HUD labels, feedback captions.
- Scenario sender names, prompt text, and reply copy while preserving two options and score/damage fields.
- Mood emoji mappings and iconography.
- Color variables, gradients, particles, portal rings, silhouettes, stickers, and procedural props.
- Approved remote audio/GIF mappings from catalogs if later stages need media changes.
- Procedural canvas background art behind the phone/chat frame.
- Conceptual five-level framing through world identity and presentation.

### Avoid
- Adding new choice counts, timers, inventory, aiming, physics, movement, or alternate win conditions.
- Replacing the canvas renderer or state model.
- Reducing tap target reliability.
- Making harder stages difficult through tiny text, hidden choices, low contrast, or clutter.

# Blueprint.md

## Current game reality

The implemented game is **Bounce Parade**, a single-page full-screen canvas arcade bumper game. It has a start overlay, a score HUD, a sound toggle, a fixed mobile joystick, and a BOOST button. The player controls a round hero/float in an open procedural field. The game starts after pressing `START PARADE`; audio unlocks, the overlay fades, and the requestAnimationFrame loop continues.

The core loop is:

1. Read keyboard or joystick movement.
2. Apply acceleration to the hero.
3. Apply friction and update position.
4. Use BOOST/Space to add a large impulse in the current direction.
5. Move the camera toward the hero.
6. Let 50 NPC circles wander.
7. Resolve collisions by pushing hero and NPC apart.
8. Award score only when a collision happens at sufficient speed.
9. Draw gradient field, ground motifs, entities, particles, parallax clouds, HUD, and feedback GIFs.

There is no explicit fail state, health, timer, level select, or win condition. The score is the main success/progress feedback.

## High-level code structure

- Inline CSS defines the page background, start screen, HUD, joystick, action button, and mobile layout.

- Inline media elements define a data-URI hero sprite and approved remote audio/GIF sources.

# Blueprint

## Current game reality

The current game is **Signal Shards**, a single-file HTML5 canvas puzzle. It uses inline CSS, inline JavaScript, remote audio elements, two remote GIF feedback images, and a full-window canvas. The player starts from a panel, enters a `PLAYING` state, drags polygon shards around the canvas, and completes a level when all shards have snapped into the central silhouette.

### High-level code structure

- `index.html`
  - CSS variables and responsive panel/HUD styling.
  - `game-config` script containing editable knobs: `snapDistance`, `primaryColor`, `secondaryColor`, and `bgSpeed`.
  - Audio elements for BGM, snap, win, start, UI, and fail.
  - UI layer with start screen, level-complete screen, HUD, and compact GIF feedback.
  - Inline JavaScript that owns state, audio unlock, geometry generation, pointer input, drawing, particles, win handling, UI buttons, and the `requestAnimationFrame` loop.

### Game loop / state model

The state sequence is:

```text
START -> PLAYING -> WIN -> PLAYING(next level)
```

The animation loop runs continuously and draws the background, target silhouettes, shards, and particles. UI panels determine whether the player can begin or continue.

### Player goals and interaction pattern

The player drags each scattered triangular shard into the central target. Releasing within `snapDistance` locks that shard. Releasing outside the distance gives fail feedback but does not end the game. Locking every shard wins the level.

### Core systems

- Responsive full-screen canvas sizing.
- Random polygon/shard generation based on level.
- Pointer/touch drag with approximate piece hit testing.
- Distance-based snap lock.
- Particle feedback.
- Audio unlock and fallback synth.
- HUD and win/next panel.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape

This is a forgiving one-screen spatial assembly puzzle, closest to a tangram/jigsaw-lite drag-and-snap game. It is not a shooter, runner, survival game, or combat game.

## Current identity summary

The source identity is neon sci-fi signal repair: shards, nodes, uplinks, blue/pink glow, and abstract grid ambience.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The active remix prompt is **“rick and morty.”** The safe trajectory is to reinterpret the game as a chaotic portal repair puzzle: the shards become unstable portal calibration fragments, the target becomes a portal core, levels become dimensions, and feedback becomes multiverse science sparks. - requestAnimationFrame main loop

- piece hit-test and snap-distance model

- next-level button increments level and regenerates pieces
- no terminal fail/death state
- mobile touch-action none on canvas

### Change safely

- title, subtitle, instructions, HUD wording, win button wording
- color variables and canvas fill/stroke colors
- particle colors and background motif drawing
- piece facial/character decoration inside existing drawShape
- center outline styling
- audio labels and catalog-approved remote URLs if needed
- feedback GIF choices from catalog if later replacement is needed
- conceptual level names and messages

Later stages should first update copy, HUD framing, palette, and procedural background identity. Only then should they refine shard character styling and level-reactive visual evolution. They must not add enemies, timers, health, shooting, teleport behavior, new collision, or a new state machine.

  - Global `GAME` state for score, wanted level, active state, frame count, camera, and shake.
  - `KEYS` input booleans for left/right/gas/brake.
  - Entity arrays for `enemies`, `cash`, `particles`, `tireTracks`, and `decor`.
  - Procedural spawning, collision, scoring, rendering, and state transitions.
- Rendering is canvas-based top-down motion graphics with a camera following the player car over an infinite neon grid.

### Game loop / state model
- Screen states:
  1. Start screen with title, premise copy, and `Start Engine` CTA.
  2. Active gameplay with canvas, HUD, score, wanted stars, health bar, and touch controls.
  3. Game-over screen with final score and restart CTA.
- `gameLoop()` runs only while `GAME.active` is true.
- Each frame calls `update()` then `draw()` through `requestAnimationFrame`.
- Restart and start both reset the same protected core loop.

### Player goals
- Drive indefinitely.
- Collect cash/briefcases to increase score.
- Avoid or recover from collisions with pursuing police cars.
- Survive as long as possible while wanted level increases with score.

### Interaction pattern
- Mobile touch controls:
  - Left and right steering buttons.
  - Gas pedal.
  - Brake/handbrake button.
- Keyboard fallback:
  - Arrow keys or WASD for testing.
- Input is continuous press/release, not discrete tapping.

### Core systems
- Vehicle acceleration, drag, steering, brake-assisted sharper turns, camera follow.
- Cash spawning around the player and collection radius.
- Police spawning offscreen and AI pursuit through smooth steering toward the player.
- Collision bounce, health loss, camera shake, particles, and feedback GIFs.
- Wanted level derived from score: `Math.floor(score / 1000)`, capped at 5.
- Enemy pressure increases through max enemy count and enemy max speed based on wanted level.
- HUD updates for score, health, and wanted stars.

### Inferred genre / gameplay shape
A mobile-first top-down arcade driving chase with endless survival, collection, and escalating pursuit pressure. It is closest to a compact arcade racing/chase game rather than a mission-based driving simulator.

### Current identity summary
The current presentation is a neon crime getaway fantasy titled **VICE HEIST VI**. It uses synthwave colors, cash briefcases, police cars, wanted stars, siren cones, palm-tree decor, and heist copy.

## Intended remixed trajectory: Rick and Morty

### Remix-direction summary
Transform the same top-down chase/collection loop into a Rick and Morty-inspired interdimensional getaway:
- The player vehicle becomes a portal-hopping sci-fi saucer / garage-built cruiser.
- Cash briefcases become portal crystals, Mega Seeds, plumbus crates, or unstable dimension samples.
- Police pursuers become Council patrol pods / portal cops / insectoid enforcement craft.
- Wanted stars become multiverse heat / Council alert pips.
- Health becomes ship integrity / portal stabilizer charge.
- Neon road-grid becomes an animated portal-grid multiverse map with green rifts, floating garage parts, alien skyline fragments, and reality-tear props.

The mechanics should remain the same. The game should still be about driving, collecting, avoiding, surviving, and escalating pressure.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- Canvas rendering architecture.
- RequestAnimationFrame update/draw loop.
- Player physics: acceleration, drag, turning, brake behavior, camera follow.
- Touch and keyboard input semantics.
- Cash collection radius and score/health reward semantics.
- Enemy pursuit AI, offscreen spawn concept, collision distance, bounce, damage, and game-over trigger.
- Wanted level score thresholds and its relationship to enemy pressure.
- Start, active gameplay, game-over, and restart state flow.
- Mobile HUD/control placement.

### Safe to change later
- Text labels, title, button copy, HUD wording.
- Colors, CSS variables, typography choices from approved catalog fonts.
- Canvas drawing functions for cars, collectibles, decor, background grid, particles, and feedback overlays as long as hitboxes and mechanics remain unchanged.
- Audio theming only through approved catalog URLs if downstream stages choose to remap sounds.
- Procedural background motifs and decor silhouettes.
- Names and framing of score, health, wanted level, and collectibles.

### Do not change in this stage
- No runtime fixes.
- No broad JavaScript refactors.
- No level file generation required in this inference stage.
- No browser QA required by this stage.

# Recreation Prompt

Create a mobile-first HTML5 canvas game called **Portal Social Club: Rick and Morty Rumor Run**. It should preserve the structure of a relaxed one-screen social collection game: the player enters a short name, presses a start button, then controls a small rounded avatar by tapping or clicking anywhere on the canvas. The avatar moves smoothly toward the tapped destination. Small glowing collectibles spawn around the playfield; when the avatar touches one, it disappears and the score increases by exactly one. The game has no death, no combat, no timer, no fail state, and no required win condition.

The presentation should feel like a Rick and Morty-inspired interdimensional hangout rather than an ocean tidepool. Use procedural canvas/CSS art instead of relying on stock images: green portal rings, garage-lab machinery, sci-fi tubes, citadel silhouettes, interdimensional cable scanlines, neon particles, and absurd multiverse props. The player and NPCs should remain mechanically identical to the source entities, but visually read as cute portal-mutated variants with optional sci-fi accessories such as spiky blue hair, goggles, lab collars, party cones, crowns, or strange badges. Collectibles should look like portal rumors, mega seed pings, glowing science samples, or interdimensional signal sparks.

Keep the same mobile-safe UI shape: a HUD showing avatar color, player name, and cumulative rumor/signal score; a customization drawer for colors and accessories; a chat button that opens a text input overlay; chat bubbles/log entries for the player and wandering NPCs; and clear feedback when pickups are collected or chat is sent. NPCs should wander independently and occasionally speak in short absurd sci-fi lines.

Frame progression as a five-world visual journey, not as new mechanics: Level 1 Garage Portal Mixer, Level 2 Cronenberg Cul-de-Sac, Level 3 Citadel Signal Market, Level 4 Interdimensional Cable Storm, and Level 5 Council Portal Collapse. # Blueprint — Rick and Morty Remix Inference

## High-level code structure
The current game is a single-file HTML5 canvas application in `index.html`.

- **HTML/UI:** full-screen `canvas#gameCanvas`, HUD layer, start/name overlay, customization drawer, GIF feedback overlays, and chat input overlay.
- **CSS:** responsive mobile-first layout, glassmorphism panels, start card, drawer, chat styling, target tap marker, and safe-area-aware UI.
- **Audio:** `AudioSys` starts on the start button gesture, plays remote audio where available, and falls back to oscillator tones.
- **Data/config:** `CONFIG` defines colors, hats/accessories, NPC names, and NPC chat phrases.
- **Engine:** canvas resize, utility math, `Entity` and `Plankton` classes, `handleInput`, `loop`, and UI event listeners.
- **Rendering:** the loop clears and redraws a gradient underwater/tidepool scene, plankton pickups, sorted entities, chat bubbles, and UI overlays.

## Current game reality
The implemented source game is **Tidepool Social Club**, a cozy one-screen mobile social collection toy. The player enters a name, starts the game, controls a crab-like avatar by tapping destinations, collects glowing plankton/rumor pickups, accumulates a score, chats with a simple log/input overlay, and customizes color/accessory. NPC crabs wander autonomously and occasionally speak. There is no death, win state, timer, combat, or explicit level system.

## Gameplay heuristic
The game works because it is simple and frictionless:

1. Start with a name.
2. Tap anywhere on the canvas to move.
3. Touch small glowing pickups to increase score.
4. Watch social/visual feedback.
5. Optionally chat and customize.
6. Continue indefinitely.

The mechanical center is not challenge/punishment; it is a relaxed collection-and-social-presence loop.

## Game loop / state model
- `state.running` gates the active game.
- The start button initializes audio, creates the player and six NPC entities, updates HUD identity, hides the start overlay, and starts the animation loop.
- `requestAnimationFrame(loop)` runs continuously after start.
- While running, the loop draws the background, probabilistically spawns pickups up to a cap, updates/draws pickups, checks pickup contact with the player, increments score on contact, then updates/draws all entities.

## Player goals
- Primary: collect as many rumor pickups as desired.
- Secondary: personalize the avatar.
- Social/toy goal: send chat messages and watch NPC chatter.

## Interaction pattern
- Tap/click canvas: set target destination.
- Start button: begin session and unlock audio.
- Palette/accessory drawer: non-destructive customization.
- Chat button/input/send/close: optional communication layer.

## Core systems
- Tap-to-move destination control.
- Entity interpolation toward targets.
- Random NPC wandering.
- Random collectible spawning.
- Distance-based pickup collection.
- Score HUD updates.
- Chat log and speech bubbles.
- Customization drawer.
- Audio and GIF feedback.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape
Simple one-screen arcade/social toy, closest to an avatar-world/social hub with light collection. It is not a runner, shooter, puzzle, or survival game.

## Current identity summary
Current presentation is ocean/tidepool themed: crabs, plankton, rumors, tidepool club copy, aquatic gradients, coral/foam/shell colors, and light social-club language.

## Intended remixed trajectory
The remix prompt is **“rick and morty”**. The target should become a Rick and Morty-inspired multiverse social collection game while preserving the source loop. The tidepool becomes an interdimensional garage/citadel/social hub. Crabs become portal-mutated variants. Plankton rumors become portal sparks, dimension samples, mega seed pings, or interdimensional rumors. Chat becomes multiverse comms. Customization becomes lab disguise/accessory selection.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- Tap/click destination movement.
- Entity movement speed and target interpolation.
- NPC wandering and speech cadence.
- Pickup spawn/contact/scoring semantics.
- +1 score per pickup.
- No death/fail/win semantics.
- Start/audio gesture flow.
- Chat and customization interactions.
- Single-canvas mobile-first architecture.

### Change safely
- Title, copy, HUD wording, NPC names, bot phrases.
- CSS palette and glass/HUD styling.
- Canvas background art.
- Entity visual drawing while preserving radius/position.
- Plankton visual drawing while preserving collection footprint.
- Accessory labels and shapes.
- Feedback overlay theming through approved catalog media or procedural fallback.

### Do not overinterpret
Do not add portal combat, enemies, weapons, bosses, timers, dimension damage, fail states, or complex RPG systems. The Rick and Morty identity should be expressed through procedural visuals, absurd chatter, portal motifs, sci-fi props, and five-world presentation progression, not new mechanics.

# Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

`index.html` implements **Avatar Remix Studio**, a single-page canvas avatar editor. The code is self-contained: CSS, DOM overlays, audio elements, configuration, input handling, UI state, procedural avatar data, and the render loop all live in the HTML file.

### High-level code structure
- CSS variables and responsive overlay styling define the neon studio UI.
- Audio elements load approved remote audio URLs and are controlled by a small audio/feedback system with WebAudio fallback tones.
- `gameState` has three states: `START`, `EDIT`, and `SHOWCASE`.
- Avatar state is a set of category indexes: `skin`, `face`, `shirt`, `pants`, `hat`.
- UI buttons update category/option state, randomize all parts, enter showcase, or return to editing.
- Canvas rendering draws a gradient/grid background, sparkles, the procedural avatar, interaction particles, and showcase confetti.

### Game loop / state model
The render loop runs continuously with `requestAnimationFrame`. Each frame resizes the canvas for DPR, advances time, eases rotation toward `targetRotation`, draws the background/grid, then draws the centered avatar and active effects. DOM overlays determine whether the player sees the start screen, editor controls, or showcase score screen.

### Player goals
The player builds a cosmetic avatar, inspects it by spinning/dragging, and locks it in for a randomized style score.

### Interaction pattern
- Tap `START MIXING`.
- Tap category tabs.
- Tap previous/next to cycle options.
- Tap randomize for a surprise combination.
- Drag the canvas horizontally to rotate/inspect.
- Tap `PRESENT AVATAR` to enter showcase.
- Tap `TUNE IT AGAIN` to return.

### Core systems
- Protected input system: DOM buttons plus canvas pointer drag.
- Protected state system: `START` -> `EDIT` -> `SHOWCASE`.
- Protected score system: randomized 80-99 style score on finish.
- Themable cosmetic database: category labels, option names, colors, hat/face types.
- Themable procedural rendering: avatar colors, background grid, particles, sparkles, confetti.
- Themable audio/media mapping: remote catalog audio/GIFs, fallback tones.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
This is best understood as a **dress-up/avatar creator** or **avatar world styling toy**, not an action game. It has no hazards, collisions, fail state, timer, or strategic resource loop.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The remix prompt is: **rick and morty**.

The safe target is **Portal Closet Remix Studio**: a Rick-and-Morty-inspired interdimensional wardrobe booth. The player assembles a portal-ready traveler using sci-fi body colors, expressions, tops, bottoms, and headgear; the randomize button becomes an unstable portal shuffle; the finish button becomes a style scan; the score becomes a multiverse style rating.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- All control semantics.
- The full-window canvas plus DOM overlay architecture.
- The main loop and avatar draw architecture.
- The three-state start/edit/showcase flow.
- The no-fail expressive play model.
- Randomized style score semantics.
- Mobile touch target sizes and canvas drag behavior.
- Audio unlock/fallback behavior.

### Change safely
- Title, CTA, and HUD copy.
- Category names and option names.
- Avatar colors and procedural decorative details.
- Background identity: portal garage, citadel, mutated suburb, arcade, council chamber.
- Particle/confetti palette and non-interactive motion graphics.
- Approved remote media mappings if needed.

### Do not overinterpret
Do not turn the game into a runner, shooter, survival game, quiz, or puzzle. Do not add enemies, portals as teleport mechanics, health, fail states, timers, or win/loss gates. The remix should be recognizable through presentation and procedural identity, not mechanical rewrites.

Create a mobile-first canvas survival-crafting arcade game called **Portal Salvage: Dimension C-137 Run**.

The player controls a small voxel sci-fi adventurer using a virtual joystick on the lower part of the screen. The world is a top-down procedurally generated multiverse field with walkable alien ground, blocked water/void/mountain tiles, harvestable objects, collectible drops, wandering weird creatures, and a portal entrance to a second pocket-dimension map.
