# Blueprint — Remix v4 Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` is a single-file HTML/CSS/JavaScript canvas game.
- CSS defines a mobile-first full-screen interface, start screen, HUD, crafting modal, game-over screen, feedback GIF panels, and virtual joystick styling.
- JavaScript is embedded as a module and contains configuration, audio loading, global state, procedural map generation, joystick input, movement/collision, harvesting, crafting, a tap-based smelting minigame, rendering, and game-state transitions.
- Rendering is code-native canvas art using voxel-like block primitives (`drawVoxel`) rather than image sprites for the main playfield.

### Game loop / state model
- Start screen waits for the player to tap `BEGIN`.
- `initGame()` resets inventory, tools, energy, maps, entities, player, camera, and UI.
- `loop()` runs via `requestAnimationFrame` while `state.active` is true.
- In normal play, `update()` handles energy drain, joystick movement, camera lerp, idle auto-interactions, entity AI, furnace proximity, particles, and game over.
- In `crafting_minigame` mode, the same animation loop draws a modal canvas overlay and updates a timed tap challenge.
- `modal_open` pauses normal movement/interaction while still animating particles.
- Failure is `energy <= 0`, which triggers `gameOver()`.
- There is no explicit victory screen; progression success is expressed by building tools, reaching the cave, forging copper/iron tools, and banking copper/iron before energy expires.

### Player goals
- Gather raw resources from a generated surface map.
- Craft basic tools and processed parts.
- Build a field furnace.
- Enter the cave dimension.
- Mine coal and iron.
- Complete tap-smelting minigames to forge copper and iron drilling tools.
- Survive the energy countdown and improve banked resources.

### Interaction pattern
- Mobile-first virtual joystick in the lower 40% of the screen controls movement.
- When the player is close to an entity and not moving, harvesting/collection/portal interaction happens automatically on a timed `chopRate`.
- A floating craft button opens a modal recipe list.
- Craft recipe buttons consume inventory and create tools, parts, a furnace, or launch a tap minigame.
- Smelting minigame requires tapping target circles before the timer expires.

### Core systems
- Procedural 64x64 surface map with water, sand, grass, mountains, trees, stones, copper, clay, animals, and a cave entrance.
- Procedural 32x32 cave map with walls, floor, coal, iron, boulders, and a ladder.
- Grid collision: surface allows sand/grass; cave allows floor.
- Resource-gated progression through recipes and tool requirements.
- Energy as both timer and attrition pressure, with resource drops restoring some energy.
- Canvas renderer with tile map, sorted entities, particles, floating text, and a tap-smelting overlay.
- Audio feedback using approved remote URLs already embedded in the game.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape
A medium-complexity one-screen/top-down survival-crafting arcade loop: mobile joystick exploration, proximity harvesting, resource collection, crafting gates, map transition, and short tap challenge.

## Current identity summary
Current presentation is a fantasy forge/survival theme named **Forge Run: Iron Trial**. It uses earthy forge colors, medieval/fantasy naming, and voxel-styled environment objects.

## Intended remixed trajectory: Rick and Morty
Transform the presentation into a **Rick and Morty-inspired portal salvage run** while preserving the resource-gated survival-crafting mechanics.

The player should feel like they are controlling a small procedural sci-fi character through unstable multiverse biomes, gathering bizarre parts, building portal/drill gadgets, and entering a cave-like pocket dimension to obtain rarer components. The existing surface/cave split maps cleanly to “Earth garage dimension” and “portal rift dimension.” The furnace becomes a portal workbench or micro-reactor. Tools become improvised sci-fi gadgets. Ores and crafting parts become crystals, batteries, Plumbus fibers, neutrino chips, and portal alloy.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance for downstream stages

### Preserve
- Single-file boot behavior unless later stages intentionally add CSS/JS assets safely.
- Canvas render architecture and `drawVoxel` primitive system.
- Joystick input semantics and lower-screen joystick capture.
- Proximity auto-harvest cadence and target distance.
- Map generation structure, dimensions, and collision rules.
- Energy drain, resource collection, craft costs, tool gates, furnace proximity gate, and smelting minigame semantics.
- Start/restart/modal/button flow.
- Mobile reachability of craft button and close button.

### Change safely
- Title, UI copy, recipe names, floating text, feedback captions.
- Color palette and CSS variables.
- Canvas colors, entity silhouettes, and procedural motifs.
- Entity/item visual interpretations while preserving entity type names internally.
- Background atmosphere and procedural overlays that do not alter hitboxes or movement.
- Audio labels/feedback copy, if using approved catalog URLs only.
- Conceptual five-level presentation plan through safe config/copy/visual metadata in later stages.

### Avoid
- Replacing joystick movement with keyboard/mouse-only movement.
- Changing `isValidMove`, map sizes, entity HP, recipe costs, energy drain, or minigame target/timer values in this stage.
- Adding combat enemies, weapons, quests, or new failure states.
- Using media from `assets/` except existing CSS/JS; remote media should come from catalogs only.

The current game is **Skyline Sprint**, a one-screen, side-scrolling arcade avoidance/collection game implemented entirely in `index.html`. It uses a full-window `<canvas>` for rendering and a DOM UI layer for the start screen, game-over screen, score HUD, mute button, and transient feedback overlay.

- CSS variables and responsive layout define the mobile-first full-screen play surface.

## Game loop / state model

Protected state model: `START -> PLAYING -> GAMEOVER`, with restart returning to `PLAYING`.

During play, the loop clears the canvas, draws the scrolling background, increments frames, applies gravity and boost physics, updates obstacles and collectibles, checks collisions/pickups, draws entities, and schedules the next animation frame only while `PLAYING`.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The player taps/clicks/presses Space to boost upward and must stay inside the safe gap between vertically paired obstacles. Passing an obstacle pair gives `+1`; collecting a bonus item gives `+5`. Collision or ground contact after a short starting grace causes game over.

## Current game reality

`index.html` implements **Lucha Stream Arena**, a full-window HTML/Canvas arcade survival game. The game uses a single canvas for active play and DOM overlays for menu, HUD, pause, shop, chat, and game-over states. Create a mobile-first single-screen canvas arcade boss fight called **Portal Panic: Morty vs the Rick-Bot**.

The player controls a nervous Morty-like hero with one input: tap or click to jump, and tap once more in midair to double jump. Use a ring-style survival buffer renamed and presented as glowing portal shards or mega seeds. # Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` is a self-contained browser game.
- CSS defines a mobile-safe full-screen canvas shell, HUD, start screen, end screen, reaction GIF overlay, and responsive UI panels.
- Inline JavaScript owns all gameplay, rendering, input, audio, state transitions, collision handling, score/ring tracking, and win/loss outcomes.
- No external JavaScript modules are imported. Existing remote audio/GIF/font URLs are catalog-approved according to embedded agent notes and should remain stable unless later stages intentionally replace them from catalog files.

### Game loop / state model
- `loop()` runs continuously with `requestAnimationFrame`, calls `update()`, calls `draw()`, then increments `frames`.
- `gameState` values are `START`, `PLAY`, `GAMEOVER`, and `VICTORY`.
- `resetGame()` starts play, initializes hero/boss/rings/score/projectiles/particles, shows HUD, hides menus, and starts loop audio.
- End states show the end screen with either defeat or victory copy and score.

### Player goals
- Primary goal: defeat the boss by reducing boss HP from 1000 to 0.
- Secondary survival goal: keep rings available as a damage buffer.
- Secondary scoring goal: earn score from boss damage and collected rings.

### Interaction pattern
- Tap/click/pointer down on the canvas to jump.
- The hero can jump from the ground and double jump once in air.
- The player times jumps to:
  - land on the boss from above while spinning,
  - land on bombs from above to kick them back toward the boss,
  - collect rings drifting across the scene,
  - avoid touching bombs or the boss from unsafe angles.

### Core systems
- Protected canvas render loop.
- Gravity-based vertical hero movement and fixed left anchor correction.
- Boss floating pattern.
- Periodic bomb spawning from boss.
- Bomb bounce physics and kicked-bomb state.
- Circular collision for hero/bombs/rings and rectangular boss proximity checks.
- Ring-based damage buffer.
- Boss HP/scoring/win-loss state machine.
- Audio fallback system and remote media elements.
- Mobile-first single tap input.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
A one-screen mobile arcade boss-fight platformer with light runner/platform timing, projectile reflection, survival buffer collection, and score chasing.

### Current identity summary
The current presentation is Sonic-inspired but genericized as “Blue Rush vs Egg Boss”: a turbo hedgehog-like hero fights an Egg Boss mech in a bright checkerboard running landscape.

### Remix-direction summary: Rick and Morty
The safest intended trajectory is to transform the game into a Rick and Morty themed portal-boss arcade fight without changing the input, physics, collision, scoring, or state machine:
- Hero becomes Morty in a portal-charged jump bubble / panic sprint silhouette.
- Boss becomes Rick’s malfunctioning portal-gun mech or a Council/Rick-bot cockpit.
- Rings become portal shards or mega seeds.
- Bombs become unstable portal cores/plumbus mines.
- Ground becomes a scrolling multiverse platform/portal lab floor.
- Background becomes animated portal dimensions across five conceptual levels.

### Preserve-vs-change guidance
Preserve:
- Tap/double-jump input semantics.
- Hero gravity, jump velocities, max jumps, fixed left-side positioning behavior, and invulnerability behavior.
- Boss HP, bomb spawn cadence, bomb kickback logic, damage values, ring damage buffer, score semantics, win/loss semantics, and state names.
- Canvas architecture and requestAnimationFrame loop.
- HUD layout placement and mobile CTA sizing.

Change safely in later stages:
- Text/copy labels.
- CSS color variables, panel treatment, start/end screen theme.
- Canvas drawing colors and shapes for hero, boss, bombs, rings, terrain, and background.
- Non-interactive particle colors and reaction captions.
- Conceptual level copy and visual world states.
- Audio/GIF selections only from catalogs if replacement is needed.

Avoid:
- Do not add lateral movement, aiming, weapons, inventories, menus, portals that teleport, or puzzle systems.
- Do not change collision thresholds or damage values for theme alone.
- Do not replace the responsive full-screen layout with a heavy DOM scene.

# Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

The working clone contains a single-file `index.html` game titled **Neon Card Empire**. It is a full-viewport canvas card game with absolutely positioned HTML/CSS UI overlays. The core play is blackjack-like: the player taps to start, deals a fixed $50 hand, chooses **Hit** or **Stand**, compares against a dealer who draws until 17+, receives a result, and returns to the betting state. A nightly tycoon layer sits on top: the player may close the floor, resolve passive income minus overhead, buy properties, and advance to the next night. Bankruptcy after overhead produces the game-over state.

## High-level code structure

- Inline CSS defines mobile-safe full-screen layout, glass HUD panels, buttons, shop modal, start screen, and game-over overlay.
- Inline audio/image declarations provide editable media slots and reaction GIF slots.
- `AudioManager` loads remote audio, unlocks on interaction, plays BGM/SFX, and synthesizes fallback sounds.
- `Game` owns state, economy variables, deck/hands, particles, floating texts, resize handling, event binding, update loop, and canvas rendering.
- Canvas rendering is procedural: scrolling skyline background, neon table, card backs/fronts, particles, and floating result text.

## Game loop / state model

`START` -> `BETTING` -> `PLAYER_TURN` -> `DEALER_TURN` -> `RESULT` -> back to `BETTING`; optional `SHOP` resolves night income/overhead and purchases; `GAMEOVER` occurs if cash is negative after shop resolution.

## Player goals

1. Win card rounds to grow cash.
2. Avoid busts and losses that drain the fixed bet.
3. End nights when appropriate, pay rising overhead, and buy income-generating properties.
4. Survive as many nights as possible while expanding the empire.

## Interaction pattern

Mobile-first button tapping: Deal, Hit, Stand, Close Floor & Expand, Buy, Open Next Night, Rebuild. Keyboard starts the game only. The remix must keep button semantics, reachability, and readable labels.

- Dealer hidden card and dealer autoplay threshold.

# Blueprint — Rick & Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
- `index.html` is a self-contained HTML/CSS/JavaScript canvas game.
- CSS defines the full-screen mobile-safe layout, sci-fi glass HUD, settings modal, feedback GIF layer, and responsive controls.
- Inline configuration lives in `<script id="game-config" type="application/x-game-config">` with safe exposed knobs: gravity, friction, initial particle count, and particle/theme color.
- JavaScript owns:
  - canvas sizing through `ResizeObserver`;
  - particle class rendering and updates;
  - pointer input for continuous particle spawning;
  - N-body gravity, friction, boundary bounce, and elastic collision resolution;
  - HUD counters;
  - time-scale controls;
  - pulse/reset/color/settings controls;
  - Web Audio / HTML audio feedback;
  - vibration bridge and GIF/status overlays.

### Game loop / state model
The game starts directly in `PLAYING` with `timeScale = 1`. `requestAnimationFrame(loop)` repeatedly:
1. Computes bounded delta time.
2. Runs one or more `physicsStep` passes depending on `timeScale` (`0`, `1`, `2`, or `3`).
3. Draws the playfield background, input reticle, and all particles.
4. Requests the next animation frame.

The practical state surface is one playable canvas plus an optional settings modal. There is no win screen, no loss screen, and no explicit level selector in the current implementation.

### Player goals
The player informally grows and manipulates a particle swarm. Score is the total swarm mass, currently equal to particle count because every particle has mass `1`. The player goal is sandbox/score-chase: create more particles, watch orbital/collision behavior, change color, pulse the swarm, and control simulation speed.

### Interaction pattern
- Touch/click and drag on the canvas to spawn particles continuously at the pointer.
- Tap `SIGNAL` to cycle the next particle color.
- Tap `HOLD`, `1X`, `2X`, or `3X` to pause or accelerate simulation time.
- Tap `PULSE SWARM` to apply random impulses to existing particles.
- Tap `RESET FIELD` to clear the swarm and restart with configured initial count.
- Tap `CONTROL DECK` to open settings, then change graphics or audio and close.

### Core systems
- N-body mutual attraction between all particles.
- Elastic particle contact resolution with impact audio/feedback.
- Screen-edge bounce containment.
- Continuous pointer-driven spawning.
- Time scaling by repeated physics substeps.
- Visual quality modes.
- Audio and vibration feedback.
- HUD score/count display.

### Inferred genre / gameplay shape
The source is best described as a one-screen physics sandbox / particle collider toy with arcade-like score feedback, not a traditional win/loss game. It has a medium-heavy physics loop but a simple input model.

### Current identity summary
The existing presentation is a neon sci-fi micro-collider: dark space gradients, glowing particle comets, glass HUD panels, technical labels (`SWARM`, `ORBS`, `CONTROL DECK`), and electronic audio.

## Intended remixed trajectory: Rick & Morty

Transform the micro-collider into a Rick & Morty-inspired multiverse portal swarm toy while preserving the simulation. The particles become portal sparks, unstable dimension seeds, plumbus fragments, micro-meeseeks, or portal foam. The pointer becomes Rick's portal gun beam / Morty's panic beacon. The HUD becomes a garage lab console. Backgrounds become procedural, animated interdimensional scenes: garage, portal highway, Council citadel, Cromulon void, collapsing multiverse.

This should be recognizable through:
- neon green portal rings;
- toxic sci-fi liquid accents;
- garage-lab junk silhouettes;
- cartoon sci-fi silhouettes for Rick/Morty-like companions without depending on copyrighted image assets;
- portal glyphs, dimensional coordinates, oscilloscopes, and absurd labels;
- five staged dimension-jump worlds.

## Preserve vs change guidance

### Preserve
- Pointer spawning semantics and spawn rate.
- Particle mass/radius/count scoring semantics.
- N-body gravity and collision model.
- Boundary bounce containment.
- Time-scale button behavior.
- Pulse/reset/signal/settings controls.
- HUD update mechanics.
- Mobile full-screen canvas and safe-area control layout.
- Audio enable/disable behavior.
- Existing runtime lifecycle and requestAnimationFrame loop.

### Safe to change downstream
- Title and UI copy.
- CSS colors, fonts from approved catalog URLs, panel styling, button labels.
- Canvas background drawing visuals.
- Particle drawing shape/color accents as long as radius/collision behavior does not change.
- Feedback labels/GIFs selected only from approved catalogs.
- Audio URLs only from approved `catalogs/audios.json` remote URLs.
- Procedural props, silhouettes, portal rings, and decorative overlays.
- Conceptual level labels and presentation-only progression layers.

### Do not overinterpret
Do not convert this into a platformer, shooter, runner, narrative choice game, combat game, or objective-based mission system unless a later stage implements only safe presentation hooks. The source mechanic is a physics swarm sandbox; the remix should make it feel like Rick & Morty without changing the protected simulation.

# Blueprint — Rick & Morty Portal Bubble Panic

## Current game reality

The working game is a single-page HTML5 canvas bubble shooter titled **Sky Signal Relay**. It uses a full-viewport canvas, a small DOM UI layer, and one embedded JavaScript game loop. The player starts from a title panel, enters play, aims with drag/mouse movement, releases to launch a circular projectile, and tries to connect that projectile to same-color bubbles in a hex-offset grid. Three or more matching connected bubbles clear, score points, spawn particle/audio/GIF feedback, and may drop disconnected floating clusters for bonus score. If a non-clearing placement reaches the lower danger rows, the game enters a game-over state with a retry button.

## High-level code structure

- `index.html`
  - CSS variables and mobile-safe layout styling.
  - `<canvas id="gameCanvas">` for the gameplay scene.
  - DOM HUD, mute button, start screen, game-over screen, and feedback GIF layer.
  - Embedded asset configuration for remote images/audio/GIFs.
  - `AudioManager` class for preload, unlock, play, stop, and mute behavior.
  - `Bubble`, `Projectile`, and `Particle` classes.
  - Grid setup, match detection, cluster dropping, scoring, win reset, loss handling.
  - `update()`, `draw()`, and `loop()` as the protected game loop.
  - Mouse and touch handlers for drag-to-aim and release-to-shoot.

## Game loop / state model

The state model is intentionally small and should be preserved:

1. `START`: title/instructions visible; game waits for Start.
2. `PLAY`: canvas loop updates projectile, collision, particles, and rendering.
3. `GAMEOVER`: final score and retry button are shown.

Clearing every bubble does not show a separate victory screen; it plays combo feedback and calls `initGame()` to continue the arcade loop with a new random grid.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The player objective is to clear the bubble grid and maximize score without letting the bubble stack reach the bottom danger area. The interaction model is:

- Drag or mouse-drag anywhere on the gameplay surface to aim.
- Release to fire the current projectile upward.
- Use side-wall bounces and direct shots to place matching colors.
- Match 3+ same-color connected bubbles to clear them.
- Drop disconnected clusters for bonus points.
- Retry after game over.

## Core systems

- Hex-offset bubble grid with 8 columns and dynamic tile sizing.
- Random five-row starting layout.
- Random next projectile color from four color types.
- Projectile movement with side-wall bounce and ceiling collision.
- Distance-based projectile-to-bubble collision.
- Snap-to-grid placement.
- BFS same-color match detection.
- Roof-connected BFS for floating cluster detection.
- Score and HUD update.
- Audio and GIF feedback.
- Mobile-safe touch input and button separation.

## Inferred genre / gameplay shape

The source is best understood as a **medium arcade bubble shooter**. It is not a runner, shooter, puzzle board game, or platformer. Skill comes from spatial aiming, color matching, bank-shot planning, and avoiding bottom-row loss.

## Current identity summary

The current surface frames the game as a futuristic sky/aurora signal relay. Bubbles are signal orbs; the HUD says Relay Score; the background is a remote runner/city image with a procedural sky overlay. The presentation is already sci-fi but generic rather than specifically Rick & Morty.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The Rick & Morty remix should become **Rick & Morty: Portal Bubble Panic**, where Rick has converted the bubble launcher into a portal stabilizer and the player fires colored dimension-frequency orbs into unstable portal clusters. Matching three or more same-frequency orbs collapses portal rifts; dropping clusters disconnects unstable dimensions; reaching the bottom means the multiverse collapses into the garage.

The remix should focus on presentation, procedural art, copy, HUD language, and level/world framing. The existing mechanics already map cleanly to portal-orb matching, so core gameplay does not need to change.

## Preserve vs. change guidance

### Preserve

- Drag-to-aim and release-to-shoot input.
- Mobile touch safety and button actionability.
- Projectile speed, upward clamp, and wall bounce.
- Hex-grid math and snap behavior.
- Match-3 threshold and BFS matching.
- Floating cluster drop logic.
- Score values: 10 per match bubble, 20 per dropped bubble.
- Loss threshold and game-over semantics.
- START / PLAY / GAMEOVER state structure.
- Canvas render architecture.

### Change safely

- Title, subtitle, button labels, start/game-over copy.
- HUD labels and status chips.
- Color palette, glows, panels, and typography.
- Bubble/orb visual styling while retaining circular silhouettes.
- Background identity through procedural portals, garage props, Citadel skyline, arcade lights, or TV-static layers.
- Non-blocking particles, overlays, and feedback copy.
- Approved remote media URLs from catalogs only if replacements are needed.

### Avoid

- New controls.
- New enemies.
- New timers.
- Changed score semantics.
- Changed match threshold.
- Physics or collision rewrites.
- Rendering migration away from the existing canvas loop.
- Visual clutter that hides bubble colors, aim line, launcher, or buttons.

## Five-level remix direction

1. **Garage Portal Calibration** — base transformed Rick garage experience.
2. **Cronenberg Cloud Bank** — first escalation through mutation danger visuals.
3. **Citadel Frequency Lockdown** — full intended stack with institutional portal lockdown framing.
4. **Blips and Chitz Chaos Run** — higher pressure arcade-world presentation.
5. **Interdimensional Cable Collapse** — final readable multiverse broadcast crisis.

These levels are conceptual planning targets for downstream stages. They should be implemented conservatively through safe variants or presentation hooks only when later stages are responsible for level construction.

# Blueprint

## Current game reality

The implemented game is a compact browser-based creature creator and companion toy contained in `index.html`. It uses a full-window Canvas for animated scenes and procedural creature drawing, with DOM/CSS overlays for the start card, lab controls, HUD, reset button, and interaction buttons.

### High-level code structure

- HTML shell: `#game-container`, full-screen `<canvas>`, overlay UI, GIF feedback element.
- CSS: mobile-first fixed layout, glass panels, bottom safe-area controls, top HUD, start modal, responsive button sizing.
- JavaScript:
  - `ASSETS` for remote BGM/SFX/GIFs.
  - `AudioController` for unlock-on-interaction audio and debounced SFX.
  - state variables for `phase`, selections, cauldron color, particles, and `creature`.
  - option arrays: `SPECIES`, `COLORS`, `SIZES`.
  - rendering functions: `drawLab`, `drawRoom`, `drawCreature`, `drawParticles`.
  - behavior function: `updateCreature`.
  - event handlers for start, create, reset, pet, feed, scare, and canvas tap-to-pet.

### Game loop / state model

The game begins on a start overlay. Clicking **ENTER LAB** unlocks audio, shows the lab controls, shows the HUD, renders ingredient buttons, and starts `requestAnimationFrame(gameLoop)`. The main state is `phase`:

- `lab`: draws the cauldron/forge and selection particles.
- `room`: draws the room, updates autonomous creature behavior, draws the creature, then draws particles.

There are no win/loss states, no scoring, no timed levels, and no resource constraints.

### Player goals and interaction pattern

The player chooses one species, one color, and one size, creates the creature, then plays with it. The core interaction is button/tap driven:

1. Select creature ingredients from a horizontal strip.
2. Press **CREATE CREATURE**.
3. Observe the creature.
4. Press **Pet**, **Feed**, or **Boo!**, or tap the creature to pet it.
5. Press **New Experiment** to return to lab selection.

### Core systems

- Procedural creature renderer with different silhouettes for fox, cat/caracal, dog, and dino.
- Procedural lab and room background renderers.
- Autonomous creature state machine: idle, walk, eat, scared, happy.
- Particle feedback for selection, bubbles, hearts, and growth.
- DOM HUD and mobile-safe action controls.
- Audio and GIF feedback layered over the game.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape

The strongest current genre is **pet simulator / creature creator**, not an arcade action game. It is low-pressure and expressive: the reward is seeing a creature customized and reacting.

## Current identity summary

The current presentation is a neon creature laboratory. The interface speaks in lab terms: species, color, size, create creature, observation room. The visual identity is already sci-fi but generic: glowing cauldron, creature forge, glassy HUD, pastel observation room.

## Intended Rick & Morty remixed trajectory

The Rick & Morty remix should become a **portal-garage creature experiment**. It should feel like an irresponsible multiverse lab toy: choose portal DNA, unstable serum, and growth setting; hatch a pocket mutant; observe it in a dimensional containment room. The remix should use recognizable procedural motifs: green portal rings, garage-lab clutter, serum vats, warning stickers, dimension labels, Citadel diagnostics, arcade containment props, and portal storm effects.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve

- The two-phase lab/room flow.
- Selection semantics: one species, one color, one size.
- Create/reset/pet/feed/scare controls.
- Tap-on-creature-to-pet behavior.
- Autonomous creature states and reaction timers.
- Canvas + DOM overlay architecture.
- Mobile safe-area controls and no-scroll viewport.
- Lack of fail/win/scoring semantics.

### Change safely

- Copy and labels.
- HUD wording.
- Option names/icons as one-for-one theme mappings.
- Canvas background art.
- Creature decorative details.
- Particles and aura styling.
- CSS palette and panel styling.
- Audio/GIF choices only via approved catalog remote URLs.

### Do not overinterpret

Do not convert the game into combat, shooter, runner, platformer, puzzle, or resource-management gameplay. Rick & Morty should be a visual/narrative frame, not permission to add dangerous mechanics.

# Blueprint.md

## Current game reality

The working game in `index.html` is a single-file canvas word-search puzzle titled **Signal Sweep**. It uses a responsive full-screen canvas, an overlaid HUD, HTML audio elements, and pointer events. The player sees a generated letter grid and a target word list. The core loop is:

1. Read the target words in the HUD.
2. Drag from one grid cell to another in a straight horizontal, vertical, or diagonal line.
3. Release to submit the selected letters.
4. If the selected string or its reverse matches an unfound target, mark it found, highlight it, play success feedback, and spawn particles.
5. If it does not match, play fail feedback and briefly shake the grid.
6. When all target words are found, show a sector-clear overlay.
7. Press the restart button to advance the sector and generate a new grid.

There is no loss condition, timer, avatar, physics simulation, enemy system, or resource economy. Progression exists through a numeric `level` value and a safe word-count increase: `Math.min(3 + Math.floor(level / 2), 6)`.

## High-level code structure

- HTML shell: `#game-container`, `canvas#gameCanvas`, HUD layer, feedback stack, game-over/sector-clear overlay, audio elements.
- CSS: mobile-first HUD, panel, badge, button, scanline, and feedback styling.
- Config script: `gameConfig.gridSize`, `themeColor`, `accentColor`.
- JavaScript systems:
  - audio unlock/playback and vibration bridge calls
  - word-bank and generated grid creation
  - word placement and target tracking
  - pointer-based drag selection
  - HUD updates and overlay state
  - canvas rendering of background, grid, letters, selection pills, found highlights, particles, and shake
  - ResizeObserver-driven responsive sizing

## Game loop / state model

The state model is intentionally small: `STARTING`, `PLAYING`, and `GAMEOVER`. The animation loop runs continuously with `requestAnimationFrame`, but game actions only process when `gameState === 'PLAYING'`. `GAMEOVER` means sector complete rather than failure.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The player goal is to find all listed words. The irreducible interaction is press/drag/release across a straight line. Mobile support is central because the canvas has `touch-action: none`, pointer events are global, and UI controls are large.

## Current identity summary

The source presentation is a neon radar/signal-ops puzzle with words drawn from nature/calm vocabulary (`TREE`, `LEAF`, `NATURE`, etc.). The current visual language uses dark sci-fi panels, scanlines, blue/green glow, floating leaf-like particles, feedback GIFs, and ambient audio.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The remix prompt is **Rick & Morty**. The safest target is not to turn the game into combat or platforming, but to reinterpret the word-search grid as a portal-frequency scanner. Target words become call signs, dimensions, characters, locations, or sci-fi objects. Correct drags become locked portal coordinates; incorrect drags become portal static. Sector progression becomes a five-world multiverse sweep.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve

- Pointer drag input semantics.
- Straight-line selection and reverse-word matching.
- Generated grid and target-found progression.
- No-loss, retry-friendly failure semantics.
- Sector-clear overlay and restart-to-next-sector flow.
- Responsive canvas sizing and mobile-safe touch areas.
- Main loop/rendering architecture.

### Change safely downstream

- Copy, title, HUD labels, result text, and feedback captions.
- `WORD_BANK` vocabulary to Rick & Morty themed terms.
- Canvas background motifs from generic signal leaves to portal rings, garage props, Citadel silhouettes, and arcade tokens.
- CSS palette and panel styling.
- Procedural particle shapes and nonblocking feedback media from approved catalogs.
- Five-level visual/narrative framing.

### Avoid

- Timers, lives, enemies, combat, moving letters, nonlinear word paths, new grid physics, or rewrites of input/collision/render architecture.\n

# Blueprint — Rick & Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

`index.html` implements **Arcade Brain Sprint**, a mobile-first timed multiple-choice arithmetic quiz. The code is contained in one HTML file with embedded CSS, DOM screens, audio elements, a canvas background renderer, and JavaScript modules for `AudioSys`, `Visuals`, and `Game`.

### High-level code structure
- **HTML screens:** language select, main menu, setup, gameplay, results, ranking.
- **CSS:** utility-style classes, glass/neon panels, mobile-safe layout rules, button feedback states, reaction GIF positioning.
- **Config:** embedded `game-config` JSON for base scores and timer seconds.
- **Audio:** approved remote URLs are already used for BGM and SFX.
- **Visuals:** canvas background with gradient, mascot face, grid motion, and confetti particles.
- **Game state:** language, theme, difficulty, question count, score, question index, counts, generated questions, timer, and playing flag.
- **Persistence:** localStorage leaderboard under `qm_rank`.

### Game loop / state model
1. Pick a language.
2. Enter main menu.
3. Open setup.
4. Choose quiz lane, pace, and round count.
5. Start run.
6. For each round: show generated arithmetic prompt, present four shuffled answers, count down, resolve tap/timeout, show feedback, advance.
7. End run with score/correct/missed metrics and leaderboard entry.

### Player goals
Answer as many questions correctly as possible before each timer expires and finish with a high leaderboard score.

### Interaction pattern
All gameplay uses large DOM buttons for touch/click input. There is no movement, aiming, dragging, or collision.

### Core systems
- Question generation: random `+`, `-`, `*` equations from numbers 1–20.
- Answer generation: one correct answer plus three nearby wrong answers.
- Timer: per-question countdown, with warning SFX/visual red state at 5 seconds.
- Scoring: correct answers award points based on selected difficulty value.
- Feedback: correct/wrong button styles, confetti, shake, GIF overlays, SFX.
- Results/leaderboard: final run summary and localStorage ranking.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The Rick & Morty prompt should transform the presentation into **Rick & Morty: Portal Brain Sprint**: a chaotic portal-garage rapid quiz where each equation stabilizes a portal jump. This should be achieved through copy, HUD labels, procedural portal/lab art, green portal effects, dimension-world progression, and approved media mapping only if needed.

## Preserve vs change guidance

### Preserve
- Four-answer quiz mechanics.
- Timer and timeout semantics.
- Score values and leaderboard semantics.
- Screen flow and mobile touch targets.
- Canvas + DOM rendering architecture.
- Existing audio unlock behavior.

### Change safely
- Title, labels, and mission copy.
- Theme labels and player-facing quiz-lane framing.
- Canvas background motifs and colors.
- Mascot/character silhouettes as procedural shapes.
- HUD naming: score as portal fluid, time as stability, progress as dimension jumps.
- Feedback visuals: correct = portal sparks, wrong = unstable dimension shake.

### Do not overinterpret
Rick & Morty theming does not imply combat, platforming, shooting, physics, enemies, or exploration. The game remains a timed quiz.

# Blueprint — Remix v4 Inference Plus

## Current game reality

The working clone contains a single-file HTML5 canvas arcade game in `index.html`. It presents itself through mixed legacy/current branding (`Trash Panda: Trash Blaster` in the document title and `MEME MELTDOWN` in the visible start card). The actual implementation is a vertical, single-screen auto-shooter:

- A player avatar stays near the bottom of a full-screen canvas.
- Mouse or touch drag controls only the horizontal target position.
- The player automatically fires upward on a cooldown.
- Enemies spawn at the top and descend.
- Three enemy roles exist: a one-hit basic enemy, a two-hit slower enemy, and a faster/weaving enemy.
- Projectile/enemy collisions award score.
- Enemy/player collisions remove health.
- Three health hearts are shown.
- Game over occurs when health reaches zero.
- Restart reinitializes the same loop.

The game has start, play/HUD, hit/fail feedback overlay, and game-over screen states. It does not have explicit authored levels, collectibles, menus, pause, shops, upgrades, or a terminal victory condition. Progression is implicit and endless: score increases spawn pressure and enemy speed.

## High-level code structure

`index.html` includes:

1. CSS variables, layout, mobile-safe panels, HUD, and GIF overlay styling.
2. DOM structure for canvas, start screen, game-over screen, HUD, hearts, and reaction GIF wrappers.
3. Embedded JavaScript:
   - `ASSETS` remote audio/GIF URL mapping.
   - `AudioController`.
   - canvas setup and resize.
   - pointer/touch input.
   - game state variables and configs.
   - enemy configuration.
   - spawn/update/collision/damage functions.
   - canvas draw functions for background, enemies, player, particles.
   - `gameLoop`, `gameOver`, start and restart event bindings.

## Game loop / state model

The protected loop is:

`start click -> audio prime/play -> hide start -> show HUD -> gameActive=true -> initGame -> requestAnimationFrame loop`

During each frame:

1. increment `frame`
2. spawn enemy if current frame matches score-adjusted rate
3. move player toward `targetX`
4. auto-fire if cooldown allows
5. move projectiles
6. move enemies and apply weave
7. resolve enemy/player collision
8. resolve projectile/enemy collision
9. update score/HUD/particles/shake
10. draw background/entities/particles
11. request next frame while active

`gameOver()` stops BGM, plays fail SFX, hides HUD, shows final score, and waits for restart.

## Player goals and interaction pattern

The goal is high-score survival. The player does not aim independently and does not press a fire button. They drag horizontally to align the auto-firing avatar under enemies while avoiding contact. Moment-to-moment challenge is spatial alignment plus timing pressure from descending hazards.

## Core systems

- Horizontal drag input.
- Smoothed player movement.
- Automatic firing.
- Random enemy spawning.
- Enemy movement and weaving.
- AABB collision.
- Health/damage/game-over.
- Score/HUD.
- Canvas procedural drawing.
- Particles, shake, GIF overlays, and audio feedback.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape

The game is best described as a compact vertical auto-shooter / wave-defense arcade survival game. It shares traits with space shooters and simple lane-defense games, but it is not a runner, platformer, puzzle, or simulator.

## Current identity summary

Current presentation is meme/feed/trash-cleanup themed: the visible copy frames the player as defending a chaotic meme feed from moderators/cleanup tools. The player sprite is a trash panda-like character; enemies are cleaning tools; the background resembles a scrolling road/lane.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The active user remix prompt is `Rick & Morty`. The safe trajectory is not to invent a new game, but to reinterpret the same auto-shooter as a portal-science multiverse survival scene:

**Portal Panic: Rick & Morty Multiverse Blaster** — a Rick-like scientist and nervous teen sidekick ride a garage-built portal sled at the bottom of the screen and automatically blast descending portal parasites, citadel drones, mutation pods, and dimension wisps. The player drags the sled horizontally to line up shots and keep the multiverse breach from reaching them.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve

- Full-screen canvas architecture.
- RequestAnimationFrame game loop.
- Horizontal drag/touch input.
- Player interpolation and bottom anchoring.
- Automatic projectile firing.
- Enemy spawn cadence and score-based ramp unless a later validated level variant safely tunes it.
- Enemy hp/speed/weave role semantics.
- AABB collision model.
- Score and health semantics.
- Start, game-over, and restart flow.
- Mobile safe areas and large buttons.

### Change safely

- Title/copy/HUD labels.
- CSS palette, fonts, panel styling, glow treatment.
- Canvas-drawn player/enemy/background silhouettes.
- Particle colors and non-colliding visual motifs.
- GIF labels or approved remote decorative feedback.
- Conceptual five-level world framing.
- Background parallax and procedural portal ambience.

### Avoid

- Manual fire or extra buttons.
- New physics.
- New pickups/upgrades/economy.
- Hitbox or collision rewrites.
- Broad JS refactors.
- Visual effects that hide enemies/projectiles.
- Non-catalog remote media or local media from `assets/`.

# Blueprint

## Current game reality
The workspace contains a single-file HTML5 Canvas game, `index.html`, titled **Style Shuffle Studio**. It is a one-screen dress-up / styling toy rather than a traditional challenge game. The code structure is:

- CSS variables, responsive UI, start overlay, feedback HUD, and bottom control panel.
- Embedded JSON config for theme, skin, and hair colors.
- Remote audio element and in-script audio manager.
- Canvas setup and resize handling.
- Runtime state: `START` and `PLAY`.
- Character state: four visible outfit/accessory toggles plus colors, blink timer, and idle animation.
- Interaction handlers for start, four outfit buttons, and Quick Mix.
- Canvas render loop for background, avatar, particles, and idle animation.

## Game loop / state model
The canvas loop always draws the animated background and avatar. In `START`, an overlay invites the player to tap. On start, the overlay hides, the control panel appears, feedback plays, and the player can toggle outfit pieces or use Quick Mix. There is no score, win state, loss state, timer, collision, physics, or enemy behavior.

## Player goals and interaction pattern
The player experiments with a character look by turning TOP, BOTTOM, SHOES, and BOW on/off. Quick Mix randomizes outfit colors and restores all pieces to ON. The loop is expressive and cosmetic: input changes avatar state, UI button state, feedback text/GIF, particles, and sound.

## Current identity summary
The current presentation is a pastel fashion studio with a cute avatar, boutique UI, glam particles, and dressing-room language.

## Intended remixed trajectory
For the **Rick & Morty** remix prompt, the safe target is **Portal Shuffle Studio**: a chaotic sci-fi multiverse styling lab where the player prepares a portal traveler for unstable dimensions. The four existing toggles become lab/portal outfit components, and Quick Mix becomes a multiverse wardrobe scramble. The remix should evoke green portals, garage-lab gadgets, alien dimensions, citadel consoles, absurd sci-fi props, and cartoon chaos through procedural canvas/CSS art.

## Preserve vs change guidance
Preserve the start flow, bottom touch controls, four independent toggles, Quick Mix randomizer, no-loss toy semantics, render loop architecture, and mobile layout. Change copy, colors, procedural background, avatar silhouette details, accessory mapping, particles, and HUD styling. Do not add combat, navigation, collision, score, timers, or failure semantics.

# Blueprint — Rick & Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality
- **Inferred genre / archetype:** one-screen / side-scrolling arcade runner
- **Core player goal:** stay alive through the scrolling challenge while collecting/earning score
- **Core verb:** move or jump with precise timing to avoid hazards and collect rewards
- **Fail state:** collision with hazards, missed recovery windows, or depleted lives/time
- **Input model:** mouse/touch/pointer
- **Rendering/camera assumption:** Canvas-centered one-screen playfield or Canvas-like update/render loop
- **Moment-to-moment loop:** read the playfield, perform the existing action/movement input, avoid/handle hazards, pursue rewards or score opportunities, receive HUD feedback, and restart/continue after failure.
- **Likely screen states:** load/title or start state, active play, pause/restart/menu state if buttons exist, game-over/result state.
- **Existing progression:** Some level/stage/wave markers were detected and should be preserved/reinterpreted.

## High-level code structure
The source appears to be a self-contained `index.html` game. Static inspection found these implementation markers:

# RecreationPrompt.md

Create a mobile-first one-screen arcade chase called **Portal Pursuit 100**. It should feel like a Rick & Morty-inspired dimensional pursuit built on a simple vertical chase shooter loop.

The player pilots a small procedural saucer containing two tiny readable silhouettes: a spiky-haired mad scientist and a nervous round-headed co-pilot. The saucer sits near the bottom of a full-screen portrait-friendly canvas. The target is a rogue Council portal rig near the top of the screen. The player controls only horizontal movement by dragging left or right on the canvas. The saucer automatically fires twin plasma bolts upward; there is no manual shooting button. The target sways laterally, drops falling square-ish portal junk, and can be disabled by repeated hits.

Preserve the core gameplay exactly: start screen, play state, game-over/win screen, drag-only horizontal steering, automatic twin shots, falling debris hazards, health/hull damage on debris collision, enemy HP reduction on bullet hits, distance progress to 100, alternate win by enemy HP reaching zero, loss by player HP reaching zero, and restart. Keep the collision model, health/damage semantics, score semantics, and input semantics stable.

Transform the presentation into a procedural Rick & Morty-style multiverse road trip. Use Canvas/CSS art rather than relying on stock images: green portal spirals, garage tools, flask bubbles, Citadel tower silhouettes, Council badges, Cronenberg blobs, Interdimensional Cable scanlines, glitchy TV frames, and a golden Central Finite Curve finale. # Blueprint.md — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

`index.html` implements **Highway Interceptor 100**, a one-screen vertical highway chase shooter. The player starts from a modal, enters a full-window Canvas play state, drags horizontally to steer a police cruiser, and automatically fires twin shots upward at a black van. The van sways left/right and drops debris. Debris collision subtracts player HP; bullet collision subtracts enemy HP. The run succeeds when pursuit distance reaches 100 miles or the enemy HP reaches zero, and fails when player HP reaches zero.

### High-level code structure

- Inline CSS defines mobile-first full-screen layout, HUD panels, neon styling, siren overlay, and responsive modal sizing.
- `game-config` JSON exposes `heroSpeed`, `gameSpeed`, `themeColor`, and `gameTitle`.
- Hidden inline SVG image placeholders supply player and enemy vehicle sprites.
- Remote audio and GIF elements provide optional feedback; WebAudio synthesis falls back if audio fetch/decode fails.
- JavaScript initializes config, audio manager, canvas, entities, input handlers, `requestAnimationFrame` loop, update/draw routines, init/end state transitions, and UI bindings.

### Game loop / state model

- States: `START`, `PLAY`, `GAME_OVER`.
- `gameLoop(timestamp)` calls `update(dt)` and `draw()` every frame.
- `update()` only mutates gameplay during `PLAY`.
- `initGame()` resets player/enemy HP, bullets, particles, obstacles, distance, shake, and visible UI.
- `endGame(win)` stops BGM, plays win/fail feedback, hides HUD, shows game-over panel, and records final distance.

### Player goals and interaction pattern

- Goal: keep the chase going to 100 miles or destroy the target before hull HP reaches zero.
- Interaction: drag/touch pointer horizontally on the canvas; there is no vertical control and no manual fire button.
- The minimum playable loop is: start → steer left/right → align shots → avoid falling debris → track distance/health → win or retry.

## Intended remixed trajectory

The user prompt is **Rick & Morty**. The safe remix trajectory is to reinterpret the existing road pursuit as a dimensional portal pursuit:

- Police cruiser → Rick-and-Morty-inspired saucer.
- Black van → rogue Council portal rig / convoy.
- Highway → dimensional freeway/portal tube.
- Miles → dimensional miles / portal run progress.
- Debris → portal junk, Citadel barricade chunks, TV shards, Cronenberg waste, golden curve fragments.
- Siren and neon HUD → portal scanner and hull integrity UI.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve

- requestAnimationFrame game loop and START/PLAY/GAME_OVER state flow
- pointer/touch drag horizontal steering
- player horizontal lerp and clamp
- enemy lateral sway/bounce behavior
- automatic twin-shot cadence
- debris drop cadence and downward movement
- bullet-enemy and obstacle-player collision semantics
- player HP/maxHp and 20 HP debris damage
- enemy HP damage of 5 per bullet
- scoreDistance time-based progress and 100-mile win threshold
- enemy HP <= 0 win threshold
- restart/init reset semantics
- mobile viewport/canvas sizing assumptions

### Change safely

- title, button text, HUD labels, game-over copy
- CSS colors, neon panel styling, type choices from approved catalogs
- Canvas drawing of road, background, player, enemy, bullets, obstacles, particles
- inline SVG placeholders for player/enemy if preserved as media-free procedural art
- audio label mapping and optional approved remote audio slots
- GIF overlay selection only from approved catalog sources if changed
- noninteractive background props and parallax layers
- level/world framing copy and conceptual progression

## Downstream heuristic

Later stages should make the game feel unmistakably like a Rick & Morty-inspired dimensional chase through procedural art, copy, and animated world design. They should not add new mechanics, new input modes, boss phases, collectibles, or collision/physics rewrites. The five-level plan should be implemented as a staged visual/world progression first, with any numeric tuning limited to existing safe config knobs only after validation.

# Blueprint: Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality
The working game is a single-file `index.html` HTML5 canvas game titled **Candy Drop**. It is a one-screen mobile-first physics puzzle in the Cut-the-Rope family.

### High-level code structure
- CSS variables and overlay styling define the candy theme, HUD, start screen, feedback GIF panel, and game-over panel.
- Inline audio elements point to approved remote sources and are managed by `AudioManager`, with synth fallback.
- `VPoint` and `VStick` implement a lightweight Verlet rope simulation.
- `Game` owns canvas sizing, state, input, level creation, physics update, collision checks, scoring, feedback, and rendering.
- The render loop is `requestAnimationFrame` and should remain intact.

### Game loop / state model
States are `START`, `PLAYING`, `WIN`, and `GAMEOVER`. The player taps from START to begin, swipes across rope segments while playing, then receives a delayed win/fail overlay and can restart.

### Player goals and interaction pattern
The player swipes to cut ropes so the candy falls or swings into the monster mouth. Optional stars add 100 points each. Failing to land in the target before leaving bounds ends the round.

### Core systems
- Pointer/touch swipe cutting
- Verlet rope constraints
- Candy gravity and momentum
- Rope segment line-intersection cuts
- Star and goal radius collision

# Blueprint — Rick & Morty Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

`index.html` contains a self-contained canvas arcade platformer titled **Zone Sprint: 10-Sector Dash**. The game uses inline CSS, HTML overlays, remote catalog-style audio/GIF URLs, and one inline JavaScript game engine.

### High-level code structure
- CSS variables and utility classes define the HUD, start screen, end screen, mobile controls, reaction cards, and responsive layout.
- Audio tags define BGM and SFX sources, with WebAudio tone fallbacks in JavaScript.
- HTML overlays provide:
  - start/menu screen
  - HUD with sector number, score `0/7`, boss HP, and super message
  - compact reaction cards
  - end screen with next/retry/menu buttons
  - mobile D-pad and jump button
- JavaScript defines:
  - config and level theme arrays
  - audio unlock/playback helpers
  - `STATE` flow: MENU, PLAY, TRANSFORM, BOSS, GAMEOVER, LEVEL_COMPLETE
  - player physics and held-input controls
  - procedural collectible, obstacle, decor, cloud, terrain, particle, player, enemy, and boss rendering
  - collision, scoring, transformation, boss, win/loss, and progression logic

## Game loop / state model
`requestAnimationFrame(loop)` runs `update(safeDt)` and `draw()` continuously. The update loop is gated by state:
- MENU/GAMEOVER/LEVEL_COMPLETE: frame counter advances but gameplay physics pause.
- PLAY: camera follows the player; physics, roll/jump, obstacles, collectible collisions, and transformation trigger run.
- TRANSFORM: a timed pause sets `player.super = true`, creates the boss, shows boss HUD, and switches to BOSS.
- BOSS: boss hovers near the camera, collision attacks reduce boss HP, and sector/campaign completion occurs.

## Player goals
1. Start the run.
2. Traverse the horizontal sector.
3. Collect all 7 energy rings.
4. Survive spikes and badniks.
5. Trigger super mode.
6. Hit the hovering Interceptor Core until HP reaches zero.
7. Advance through sectors up to the campaign clear.

## Interaction pattern
- Keyboard: ArrowLeft / ArrowRight / ArrowDown / Space.
- Mobile: left/right/down D-pad buttons and a separate JUMP button.
- Inputs are held booleans. Down while grounded and moving makes the player roll; Space jumps when grounded.

## Core systems
- Momentum platform movement.
- Procedural stage generation.
- AABB collision.
- Collectible score gate.
- Transformation and boss phase.
- Existing 10-sector progression with difficulty scaling.
- Canvas procedural rendering.
- HUD and modal overlays.
- Remote audio + WebAudio fallback.

## Inferred genre/gameplay shape
Medium arcade side-scrolling speed platformer with runner-like flow and a boss-fight capstone per level.

## Current identity summary
The current source identity is a Sonic-inspired sci-fi sprint: blue spiky hero, rings/emeralds, badniks, spikes, colorful zones, and a hovering boss.

## Intended remixed trajectory
The remix prompt is **Rick & Morty**. The target should become **Rick & Morty: Portal Sector Sprint**: a chaotic multiverse sprint where the player collects portal charges, survives unstable dimensions, transforms into an overcharged portal state, and defeats Council/Federation interceptors.

### Preserve
- Main loop and state machine.
- Input semantics and mobile button behavior.
- Movement physics, roll, jump, acceleration, gravity, friction.
- AABB collision model.
- 7-collectible scoring gate.
- Boss HP/contact/invulnerability semantics.
- Existing progression hooks and win/loss rules.
- Mobile-safe layout.

### Change safely

- Audio mapping only through approved catalog sources.

## Five-level planning summary
The later visual stages should express five recognizable Rick & Morty worlds:
1. Garage Portal Calibration
2. Cronenberg Suburb Spillover
3. Citadel Traffic Loop
4. Blips & Chitz Quantum Arcade
5. The Curve Collapse

These five worlds should use the existing level progression mechanics, not new mechanics.

# Blueprint — Remix Inference Plus

## Current game reality

### High-level code structure
The current game is a compact single-file browser arcade game in `index.html`. It contains:
- Embedded HTML for the title screen, HUD, game area, player ship, overlay, and control buttons.
- Embedded CSS for a neon space presentation, responsive sizing, HUD styling, player/object visuals, and mobile-friendly layout.
- Embedded JavaScript for game state, spawning, collision checks, scoring, lives, levels, pause/restart flow, mouse/touch input, and the `requestAnimationFrame` loop.

No external images or audio are required by the current implementation. The active visuals are CSS gradients, DOM elements, emoji-like symbols/classes, and motion through DOM positioning.

### Game loop / state model
The game is `Wormhole Dash`, a one-screen vertical dodge-and-collect arcade loop:
1. The player starts a mission from the intro surface.
2. The player ship stays near the lower portion of the playfield and follows horizontal pointer/touch position.
3. Falling objects spawn at the top of the game area.
4. Portal objects are rewards; colliding with them adds score and removes the portal.
5. Meteor objects are hazards; colliding with them removes one life and removes the meteor.
6. Reaching the score target wins the current level.
7. Losing all lives triggers game over.
8. If the player wins below level 5, the "next level" flow advances the level and resumes with more pressure.

### Player goals
- Primary goal: collect enough portal rewards to reach the level score target.
- Secondary goal: avoid meteors to preserve lives.
- Progress goal: clear up to five levels.

### Interaction pattern
The player does not directly jump, shoot, accelerate, or steer with velocity. The core input is direct horizontal positioning:
- Mouse movement sets player X on desktop.
- Touch movement sets player X on mobile.
- Buttons handle start, pause/resume, restart, and next level.

### Core systems
- Pointer/touch horizontal player control.
- Timed random object spawning.
- Reward/hazard object classification.
- DOM element movement with falling Y coordinate.
- Bounding-box collision.
- Score/lives/level HUD.
- Win/loss overlay.
- Level progression through five stages.
- Pause/resume state.

### Inferred genre/gameplay shape
The source game is best described as a simple one-screen arcade dodge-and-collect / lane-runner-adjacent space game. It has no lane locking, shooting, physics simulation, inventory, or map exploration. Its complexity comes from timing, spatial positioning, spawn density, falling speed, and distinguishing hazard/reward objects quickly.

### Current identity summary
The current identity is generic neon space: a ship collects portals while avoiding meteors during a wormhole dash. The visuals are readable and lightweight but not strongly authored beyond space/portal motifs.

## Intended remixed trajectory: Rick & Morty-inspired portal chaos

The remix should reinterpret the existing mechanics as a Rick & Morty-style multiverse portal run without changing the protected game loop. The player becomes a tiny flying saucer/portal cruiser piloted through chaotic dimensional lanes. Collectibles become glowing green portal fluid/portal rings/interdimensional crystals. Hazards become meteors, broken portal shards, unstable alien debris, and federation-like drones. The background becomes a procedural garage-to-multiverse journey with portal rings, floating dimensions, alien silhouettes, and green sci-fi energy.

This should be an homage-like sci-fi cartoon multiverse direction rather than a dependency on copyrighted image assets. Later visual stages should use code-native CSS/SVG/DOM art to produce recognizable cues: green portals, mad-science gadgets, saucer silhouettes, spiky alien planets, lab/garage props, portal fluid vials, and chaotic dimensional rifts.

## Preserve-vs-change guidance

### Preserve
- One-screen dodge-and-collect arcade loop.
- Horizontal pointer/touch control.
- Falling reward/hazard objects.
- Collision model.
- Score target semantics.
- Lives semantics.
- Win/loss semantics.
- Five-level progression hook.
- Pause/restart/next-level controls.
- DOM/requestAnimationFrame rendering architecture.
- Mobile touch actionability.

### Change safely
- Title, copy, HUD labels, overlay wording.
- CSS colors, fonts, backgrounds, shadows, particles, and motif styling.
- Class names/labels only if all references remain intact; avoid unnecessary code refactors.
- Reward/hazard visual symbols and names.
- Background identity and progression cues.
- Procedural decorative elements that do not affect collision.
- Audio only if added from approved catalog sources in later stages; current audio can remain not applicable.

### Avoid
- Rewriting the main loop.
- Altering scoring/lives/progression semantics.
- Changing the input model.
- Adding new verbs such as shooting, jumping, inventory, or branching dialogue.
- Making hazards/rewards ambiguous.
- Introducing heavy external media or stock backgrounds as the main identity.
- Breaking mobile layout with unreachable controls or obscured gameplay.

## Downstream implementation priority
1. Keep `index.html` stable and mechanics intact.
2. Strengthen theme through procedural background, UI copy, and object skins.
3. Use the existing `level` variable to make visual evolution obvious across five levels.
4. Preserve gameplay readability before adding decorative chaos.
5. Validate on the assigned localhost port only in later runtime stages.

# Blueprint

## Current game reality
`index.html` implements a single-file, canvas-based arcade service game titled **Arcade Snack Rush**. The code structure is compact:

- CSS variables and responsive HUD styling in the document head.
- Hidden remote audio elements declared in `#assets`.
- A small JSON config block exposing `baseSpeed` and `themeColor`.
- A full-screen canvas plus DOM HUD and game-over overlay.
- Inline JavaScript for initialization, audio, queue state, input, update loop, drawing, scoring, game over, restart, vibration, and reactions.

The game starts directly in `PLAYING`. Customers are represented as bubbles moving down a centered lane. The player reads the front customer request and taps one of four bottom canvas buttons. Correct input awards 10 tickets, plays success feedback, removes the customer, and refills the queue. Wrong input or patience timeout subtracts one strike. At zero lives, `GAMEOVER` appears with final score and a restart button.

## Gameplay heuristic
This is a **one-screen arcade order-matching loop**. The irreducible loop is:

1. Identify the front request.
2. Tap the matching bottom button.
3. Receive score/feedback or lose a strike.
4. Repeat as patience pressure increases.

The challenge comes from recognition speed, timing pressure, four-choice target selection, limited lives, and maintaining focus on the front queue member.

## Current identity summary
The existing identity is a neon arcade snack counter. It already has polished HUD styling, remote catalog audio, reaction GIF overlays, particles, shake feedback, and mobile-safe button sizing.

## Intended remixed trajectory
The remix prompt is **Rick & Morty**. The safe remixed trajectory is **Portal Snack Rush: Dimension C-137 Counter**: Rick has turned the snack counter into a multiverse portal dispatch line, and Morty must fulfill alien portal orders before the dimension destabilizes.

The source mechanics should remain unchanged. The transformation should happen through procedural art, copy, item labels, HUD wording, background identity, customer silhouettes, portal effects, and level/world framing.

## Preserve vs change guidance
### Preserve
- Canvas loop/update/draw architecture.
- Pointer/touch input on four bottom buttons.
- Front-customer-only matching.
- Score = +10 per correct request.
- Wrong/timeout = -1 life.
- Three starting lives and game-over threshold.
- Queue refill and patience pressure.
- DOM restart behavior.
- Mobile button reachability.

### Change safely
- Title, HUD labels, hint copy, and game-over wording.
- Food/request visual identities.
- Customer bubble styling and background world.
- Particles, color palette, portal motifs, and procedural props.
- Audio/GIF mapping only if using approved catalog URLs.
- Conceptual five-level framing and level-specific world art.

## Five-level trajectory
The game does not currently expose explicit levels. Downstream stages should define five conceptual/direct variants or level configurations only through safe hooks and presentation: Garage Portal Counter, Citadel Cafeteria Queue, Cronenberg Drive-Thru, Interdimensional Cable Rush, and Council of Ricks Portal Collapse.
